# pcg-ts — agent guide

pcg-ts is a deterministic procedural content generation library for
TypeScript (browser + Node, ESM, package `pcg-ts`, optional three.js
adapter `pcg-ts/three`, optional WebGPU field evaluation `pcg-ts/gpu`,
shipped primitive vocabulary `pcg-ts/primitives`).
It combines a domain-based attribute data model
(SoA typed arrays), deferred field expressions, a memoizing node-graph
executor, and a hierarchical streaming runtime. It is designed to be
driven programmatically: node capabilities are enumerable at runtime
(`listNodeTypes()`), graphs round-trip through versioned JSON
(`serializeGraph`/`deserializeGraph`), and all errors are actionable.

Two version numbers, and they are not the same number. `VERSION` is the
released package version as a string — the only one a consumer can read
at runtime, and what `pcg --version` prints. `formatVersion` is the
serialized-graph schema version, carried in every graph document, and it
is `1`; see "Authoring a graph as JSON" for what would move it. A release
bump never touches `formatVersion`, and a graph written today states `1`
whatever `VERSION` says.

## Core mental model

- Data flows through graphs as collections of items: geometry items,
  value items (plain numbers/strings/bools), instances items (transform
  batches for renderers, each optionally carrying named per-instance
  attribute channels — colour among them, not beside them).
  Items carry tags and a revision id (`rev`).
- You BUILD those three with `makeGeometryItem(geo, tags?)`,
  `makeValueItem(value, tags?)` and `makeInstancesItem(batches, tags?)` —
  the constructor set `dataInput` names by hand when it refuses something
  ("expected a geometry, value or instances item; see
  makeGeometryItem/makeValueItem/makeInstancesItem"). Use them rather
  than an object literal of the same shape: each stamps a fresh `rev`,
  and `rev` is what the memo cache keys on instead of hashing the data,
  so a hand-rolled item reusing a number is a cache HIT on changed
  content — a stale cook with nothing to report. Binding live data into a
  graph (`graph.setParam(node, "items", [...])`) and returning outputs
  from a node implementation are the same call.
- A pin carries a COLLECTION, and one connection can put many geometries
  on it (`partitionByAttribute` emits one per distinct value; a subgraph
  or `dataInput` forwards however many it holds). A node that processes
  exactly one geometry ERRORS when handed several, rather than silently
  using the first — that would look like a successful cook. The three
  fixes, all named in the error: insert `mergePoints` to concatenate them
  back into one cloud (points-only — rebuild any path after it with
  `pointsToPath`), move the op UPSTREAM of the split so it runs once on
  the whole cloud, or put it inside a `forEach`.
- `forEach` cooks an inner graph ONCE PER ELEMENT. Built like `subgraph`,
  with one rule: exactly one exposed input must be named `each` (one
  iteration per item) or `eachPoint` (one iteration per point of the one
  geometry, the body seeing a one-point cloud). Every other exposed input
  is broadcast whole to every iteration. Outputs are concatenated in the
  iterated collection's own order and carry the iterated item's tags, so
  `partitionByAttribute` → `forEach` → `filterByTag` works end to end.
  The mode is a pin NAME, not a param, because the format is closed and a
  new key would need a `formatVersion` bump. Every iteration is seeded on
  its element's CONTENT (position bits, the `seed` attribute, the tags),
  never on its index — so reordering the input reorders the output and
  re-rolls none of it — and two elements with identical content and tags
  are refused rather than run twice. The body gets no memo reuse between
  iterations by construction (each rotates the inner seed, and a node
  holds one cache slot); the `forEach` node itself memoizes normally. To
  REPLICATE rather than iterate data, build K carriers — `pointLine`
  count K → `setAttribute` id = `index()` → `partitionByAttribute` — and
  read per-iteration constants from `randomField` on the `detail` domain.
  From TypeScript a collection is still an ordinary array:
  `collection.filter((i) => i.kind === "geometry")` gives you all of them
  and `filterByTag(collection, "<attr>=<value>")` picks one by tag.
- `repeatUntil` cooks an inner graph REPEATEDLY, feeding round k's output
  back into round k+1's input until the body stops changing anything — the
  bounded fixed point, in a graph where a cycle cannot be wired. It is the
  loop `forEach` cannot express, because the number of rounds is not known
  before the first one runs: push overlapping props apart and a new pair
  now overlaps; snap a dangling edge and the snap creates another dangler.
  Built like `subgraph`, with one rule on BOTH sides: exactly one exposed
  input and exactly one exposed output must be named `carry`. Every other
  exposed input is broadcast whole to every round. Termination is a scalar
  the body publishes on the DETAIL domain of the carried geometry, named
  by `settleAttr` (default `moves`, normally written by
  `attributeReduce`): all zero means settled, and that round counts. An
  ABSENT signal is refused by name rather than read as zero, because
  reading it as zero turns a typo into "converged on round one". Reaching
  the `maxRounds` ceiling is not an error and is not silent either — the
  two synthetic outputs `rounds` and `converged` (value items the body
  never declared) are how a host tells a settled result from a truncated
  one. The seed is NOT rotated per round, deliberately: a fixed point
  exists only if the body is the same function every round, so a body
  whose seed varies with the round re-rolls whatever the last round
  settled and reports `converged` false forever, with no error to say why.
  That constancy is also the payoff — a broadcast branch whose inputs did
  not change serves its cache instead of cooking again.
- A `Geometry` holds four attribute domains: point, vertex, primitive,
  detail (always 1 element), plus topology (vertex->point map, primitive
  vertex ranges). Point-only clouds are the common fast path. `DOMAINS`
  is those four names as a runtime array in canonical order — read it
  rather than hardcoding the list, so a "for every domain" walk cannot
  disagree with the library about what the domains are or what order
  they come in.
- Each domain is an `AttributeSet`: an ordered collection of attributes
  sharing one element count, which is what `geo.attrs.point` (and
  `.vertex` / `.primitive` / `.detail`) IS. Iteration is insertion
  order — stable and deterministic, and `rename` keeps an attribute's
  position rather than moving it to the end, so nothing that walks a
  domain depends on when a column was added.
- Attributes are named typed-array columns (f32/i32/u32/bool/string)
  with a tuple size. Standard point attributes: P (f32x3), rot (quat
  f32x4, xyzw), scale (f32x3), density (f32), boundsMin/boundsMax
  (f32x3), color (f32x4), seed (u32). `STANDARD_POINT_ATTRS` is that
  table at runtime — `{ name, type, tupleSize, defaultValue }` each, in
  the order `createPointCloud` adds them — and it is the only statement
  of the DEFAULTS, which the prose list above does not carry: rot
  `[0,0,0,1]` (identity quat), scale `[1,1,1]`, density `1`, color
  `[1,1,1,1]`, and `[0,0,0]` / `0` for the rest. A fresh cloud is not
  zeroed, and code that assumes it is will read a scale of 0 where the
  library put 1.
- What a geometry IS, before you decide what to do with it, is a
  question about its PRIMITIVES, not its point count:
  `primitiveTypeCounts(geo)` returns how many primitives carry each
  `primtype` value — `poly` for a mesh (surface sampler, triangle
  renderer), `polyline` for a path or edge network (arc-length sampler,
  line renderer). Two different things return `{}`: a geometry with no
  primitives at all, and one whose topology was set through
  `Geometry.setTopology` directly, which stamps no tag — so an empty
  record is "nothing tagged", never "no primitives". `PRIMTYPE_ATTR` is
  the attribute name (`"primtype"`, a string column on the primitive
  domain) for the cases that must read or write the tag directly;
  `primitiveTypeCounts` is the door that saves you knowing that.
- A `Field` is a deferred computation resolved per element of a domain.
  Field-capable node params accept a constant OR a field expression;
  scalars broadcast against tuples.
- Cooking pulls from declared graph outputs, topologically, memoizing
  each node on (type, param hash, node seed, input item revs).
  `cook(graph, { outputs: ["name"] })` cooks only the named outputs'
  upstream subgraph; untouched nodes keep their caches, so staged
  pipelines (cook output A, bind data, cook output B) fit in one graph.

## Authoring a graph as JSON

Format (`SerializedGraph`, formatVersion 1 — field names exactly):

- `formatVersion`: 1
- `seed`: number (graph seed; node seeds derive from it)
- `meta`: optional `{ title, description, tags }` — the only place
  descriptive text belongs; excluded from the content hash
- `params`: optional [{ `name`, `value`, `targets`?, `min`?, `max`?,
  `description`? }] —
  GRAPH-SCOPED params, in declaration order, written only when non-empty.
  One value declared once at the top level, reaching a node by one of TWO
  routes. READ: any node's field expression names it as
  `{ fn: "param", name }` with NO inline `value` (below); binding happens
  at DESERIALIZE, by substitution into the spec, so the graph cooks
  byte-identically to one with that number written out in every reading
  slot. WRITE: `targets` is [{ `node`, `param` }], param slots the value
  is written into at load, in write order — which is the only way a
  declaration reaches an `i32`, `bool`, `string`, `enum` or non-field
  vector, since every field-capable param in the registry is `f32`,
  `vec3` or `vec4` and so no expression could carry one. A targeted
  param's schema is DERIVED from the slots it drives (types and enums must
  agree, `acceptsField`/`acceptsInfinite` ANDed, bounds intersected and
  narrowable only), and a driven slot is NOT independently editable — the
  declaration wins on every load and serialization writes it back over the
  node's literal, so that literal is dead text. Refused: two declarations
  on one slot, a target that already holds a field expression, a target
  naming a missing node or param, and a node literal THE FILE ACTUALLY
  CARRIED that disagrees with its driver — a slot merely holding a
  schema default is overwritten silently, since nothing there was
  authored to object to. A declaration with neither a reader nor a target
  is legal and reported (`read by nothing`), not refused. Untargeted,
  `value` is a finite number or an array of exactly 3 or 4 of them (a
  vec3 or a vec4 — any other width is refused by name, the param
  vocabulary having nothing to call it), never a spec and never a
  reference to another param; targeted, it is whatever the merged schema
  admits. `name` may
  not contain a `.` or start with `$` (the address is `"$<name>"`). A
  declared `min`/`max` is enforced on the value, componentwise, by the
  graph itself, since a hoisted value has no spec of its own to be
  refused by. A repeated name is a hard error — it is an ARRAY rather
  than an object precisely so a duplicate is detectable, `JSON.parse`
  collapsing duplicate object keys before any reader sees them. A
  subgraph payload's graph may NOT carry it — a body's names are bound by
  its WRAPPER's exposed params, which is the one binder a body has.
- `nodes`: [{ `id`: string, `type`: registered type name, `params`: object }]
  Omitted params take their schema defaults. Field-capable params accept
  a field spec object (below) instead of a constant. A `subgraph` node
  additionally carries `subgraph: { graph, inputs, outputs, params }` —
  the inner graph recursively in this same format, the exposed pin
  mappings (`{ name, node, pin }` each), and the exposed-param
  declarations (`{ name, targets, description, default, min?, max? }`;
  `type`/`enum`/`acceptsField` are re-derived from the targets on load,
  never read from JSON, and an EMPTY `targets` derives them from
  `default`'s shape instead) — so nested subgraphs round-trip. Its own
  `params` hold the exposed params' values. INSTEAD of `subgraph` it may
  carry `ref: { name, hash? }`, referencing a subgraph registered with
  `registerSubgraph` (below); the two keys are mutually exclusive and no
  other node type may carry either. A
  `dataInput` node serializes with `items: []` (live DataItems are
  runtime-injected; re-bind after deserializing).
- `connections`: [{ `from`: [nodeId, outputPin], `to`: [nodeId, inputPin] }]
- `outputs`: [{ `id`: nodeId, `pin`: outputPin, `name`: result key }]

The key sets above are COMPLETE, at EVERY object position: the graph
object, a node object, a `subgraph` payload, a `ref`, a connection, a
declared output, an exposed-pin declaration, an exposed-param declaration
and each of its `targets`. An unknown key at any of them is a hard error
naming it and listing the valid ones. The format is closed: a future
field an old reader could MISREAD arrives with a `formatVersion` bump,
not by riding along unnoticed. An added KEY is not that case — the closed
list refuses it by name rather than ignoring it — which is why `meta` and
`params` both arrived under formatVersion 1; spend the bump on a change
to what an EXISTING key means. There is no annotation key (descriptive
text goes in `meta`, or in an exposed param's own `description`).

An exposed-param declaration carries ONLY { `name`, `targets`,
`description`, `default`?, `min`?, `max`? }. Writing `type`, `enum` or
`acceptsField` on one is refused by name: the schema is derived from the
targets' registered schemas, so a declaration cannot claim a type or a
field capability the inner params do not have.

`targets` may be EMPTY. Every exposed param also binds its name into its
body's FIELD scope, where a spec reads it as `{ fn: "param", name }`, so a
declaration with no targets still drives the cook — that is how a value
reaches a number living inside a field expression, which has no param slot
to write into. With no targets there is no inner schema to borrow: the
`default` is required and its SHAPE gives the type (a number f32, a
3-number array vec3, a 4-number array vec4, and nothing else), and the
param is always field-capable: a Field binding is SPLICED into the
expression where the reference stands, so the knob can vary per element.

That wrapper is the ONLY binder a body has: the graph inside a `subgraph`
payload may not declare a top-level `params` block, and saying so is an
error naming the two homes that work — an exposed param with no targets
on the payload, or a declaration on the OUTER graph whose value reaches
the body through the wrapper's own param slot, one hop at a time.

Complete minimal example (deserializes and cooks as-is):

```json
{
  "formatVersion": 1,
  "seed": 42,
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "scatter", "type": "pointScatterInBounds",
      "params": { "count": 500, "boundsMin": [0, 0, 0], "boundsMax": [50, 0, 50] } },
    { "id": "jitter", "type": "jitterPoints",
      "params": { "amount": { "fn": "fbm", "base": "perlinNoise", "opts": { "frequency": 0.05 } } } }
  ],
  "connections": [ { "from": ["scatter", "out"], "to": ["jitter", "in"] } ],
  "outputs": [ { "id": "jitter", "pin": "out", "name": "points" } ]
}
```

```ts
import { deserializeGraph, serializeGraph, cook, firstGeometry } from "pcg-ts";
const graph = deserializeGraph(json);      // validates everything, names faults
const result = await cook(graph);          // { outputs, stats }
const geo = firstGeometry(result.outputs.points);
serializeGraph(graph);                     // back to JSON (see round-trip note)
```

Round-trip semantics, stated precisely because agents diff JSON: the
output is semantically identical and cooks byte-identically, but it is
NOT textually equal to hand-authored input that omitted params —
serialization writes every param explicitly, filling omitted ones with
their schema defaults. It is idempotent from then on
(`serialize(deserialize(x)) === serialize(deserialize(serialize(deserialize(x))))`).
So compare round-tripped JSON against a round-tripped baseline, never
against your minimal source, and treat newly-appearing default params
as normalization rather than corruption.

## Authoring a graph in code

```ts
import { Graph, cook, pointScatterInBounds, jitterPoints } from "pcg-ts";
const g = new Graph(42);
const a = g.add(pointScatterInBounds, { count: 500 });
const b = g.add(jitterPoints, { amount: [0.5, 0, 0.5] });
g.connect(a, "out", b, "in");
g.output(b, "out", "points");
const { outputs, stats } = await cook(g); // stats: { cooked, cached, elapsedMs }
```

Two ways to get a node DEF, and they are not interchangeable.
`standardNode(spec)` REGISTERS a type under a name: that is what puts it
in `listNodeTypes()`, gives its params a schema to be validated against,
and makes a graph that uses it serializable — a duplicate name throws and
there is no unregister. `defineNode(def)` registers nothing and returns
its argument unchanged; its whole job is type inference, pinning the
def's param type `P` so that `execute`'s `params` is typed rather than
widened, which a bare object literal does not give you.
`serializeGraph` is stricter than "a registered type": it wants THE
registered def object for that type, so redeclaring a name is not a
loophole. A def you only `defineNode`d therefore builds and cooks but
cannot be saved. The wrappers are the exception and the reason the helper
exists: `subgraphNode`, `forEachNode` and `repeatUntilNode` build their
PER-INSTANCE defs with `defineNode`, because a wrapper's pins and params
come from the body it wraps and cannot be written down once in a
registered schema — and those DO serialize, because their defs carry a
recorded subgraph spec that serialization looks for before it asks the
registry anything. Build one by hand instead of through its factory and
serialization refuses it by name, pointing at the factory to use.

## Graph mutation and introspection (editor/tooling surface)

Every mutation bumps the graph version; the introspection reads are
frozen snapshots with no mutation path that bypasses version bumps.

- `graph.removeNode(handle)` — removes the node, every connection
  touching it, and every output declared on it (documented cascade); one
  version bump; the removed node's cached outputs are dropped
  immediately. Next cook: former downstream nodes recook, untouched
  branches keep serving their caches. Unknown handles (another graph's,
  or already removed) throw. Removing a subgraph *instance* leaves its
  def and inner graph intact.
- `graph.disconnect(from, "pin", to, "pin")` — removes one matching
  connection, returns `true`. Unknown nodes or pins THROW (naming the
  offender, listing valid pins); a missing connection between valid
  endpoints returns `false` with no version bump. On a `multi` input the
  remaining connections keep insertion order (order is part of
  determinism). Cache contract as removeNode: target and downstream
  recook, untouched branches stay cached.
- `graph.removeOutput(name)` — undeclares a terminal output; the name is
  free to redeclare; unknown names throw, listing declared outputs. Node
  caches untouched (outputs change what a cook pulls, not memo keys), so
  the next cook serves every unchanged node from cache.
- `graph.describe()` — frozen structural snapshot: `{ nodes: [{ id,
  seed, defType }], connections: [{ from: [id, pin], to: [id, pin] }],
  outputs: [{ id, pin, name }] }` in insertion/creation/declaration
  order. `seed` is the derived per-node seed the executor uses; `defType`
  is `undefined` when a def carries no usable type string. Cheap enough
  to call per UI frame. Reports structure verbatim — for a
  subgraph-wrapped graph that includes injected plumbing, which
  serialization excludes.
- `graph.getParams(handle)` — frozen shallow copy of the node's current
  params at call time (later setParam calls not reflected). Nested
  values are live references under the library-wide aliasing rule: treat
  them as frozen, change params only through `setParam`.
- `describeSubgraphPins(def)` — per-instance pins of a `subgraphNode`
  def: frozen `{ inputs, outputs }`, the body's exposed pins first in
  exposure order with kinds resolved live from the recorded spec through
  nested subgraphs, then any pin the WRAPPER adds on top, in the order
  the def declares them. A wrapper pin is an ordinary entry carrying
  `synthesized: true` — today only `repeatUntil`'s `rounds` and
  `converged`, since `forEach` synthesizes none. Read the flag as BOTH
  halves of the fact, because they pull opposite ways: the pin is REAL —
  it is on the def, it can be wired, and leaving it out would tell you a
  loop node has fewer outputs than it has, when those two are the only
  way to tell a settled result from one that hit `maxRounds` — but it is
  NOT the body's, so it traces to no exposed inner pin, does not move
  when the recipe's exposed outputs are renamed, and survives editing the
  body. The key is ABSENT rather than `false` on an ordinary pin, so a
  consumer comparing against `{ name, kind }` still matches the ordinary
  case exactly. A body may not expose an output named `rounds` or
  `converged` — `repeatUntilNode` refuses it outright rather than
  shadowing, which is what keeps the two sets disjoint. Returns
  `undefined` for non-subgraph defs; throws (GraphValidationError, naming
  pin and inner node) when later edits broke the wrapper.
- `describeSubgraphParams(def)` — per-instance params of a `subgraphNode`
  def: frozen list of `{ name, schema, targets }` in exposure order,
  where `schema` is the ParamSchema merged from the inner targets and
  `targets` are the `{ node, param }` slots the value is written into.
  Returns `undefined` for non-subgraph defs; throws when later edits
  removed a bound inner node or param.
- `graph.setGraphParam(name, value)` — turn one graph-scoped param
  (`graph.graphParams` reads the declared list back, frozen). Rebuilds
  every authored field spec that reads the name and installs it with
  `setParam`: the readers re-key and recook, every non-reader's param
  object is untouched and is served from cache. The declared `min`/`max`
  binds the write, componentwise. Throws naming the declared names for an
  undeclared one, and refuses a slot whose field was COMPOSED with the
  constructors around a spec (`mul(fieldFromJson(…), 3)`) — it cannot be
  rebuilt, so it would keep its old value while every authored expression
  took the new one. The writes are LOUD (they bump `graph.version`), so a
  streaming World sees a user edit rather than its own per-cell binding.
  `graph.setGraphParams(list)` declares the block and pushes nothing into
  the nodes — the deserialize path, where the fields are already bound —
  and bumps no version of its own.
- `describeGraphParams(graph)` — every param of a graph that can be
  addressed and turned: frozen-shape records discriminated by `scope`,
  the graph-scoped ones FIRST in declaration order, then the node ones in
  node order. Narrow on `scope` before reading a field: a graph-scoped
  param belongs to no node and has no `node`, `type` or `param`.
  `scope: "graph"` is `{ key: "$<name>", scope, name, readers, schema,
  value, holdsField: false, exposed: true }`, one per top-level `params`
  declaration. `key` is `"$<name>"` — one segment and a sigil, so it
  collides with neither node shape nor the editor's bare `"seed"` (a
  graph param named `seed` is addressed `$seed` and is a different knob).
  `readers` lists the `"<node>.<param>"` of every slot whose expression
  reads that name, and is EMPTY for a declaration nothing reads — legal,
  and what a rename leaves behind, which is why it is reported rather
  than refused. `schema` comes from the value's shape plus the
  declaration's own `min`/`max`/`description`, exactly as an inline field
  param's does, and `exposed` is always `true`: a top-level declaration
  is an author saying the number is worth turning.
  `scope: "node"` is `{ key, scope, node, type, param, fieldParam?,
  schema, value?, holdsField, exposed }`. `key` is `"<node>.<param>"`, or
  `"<node>.<param>.<fieldParam>"` for a literal an author wrote INSIDE a
  field expression (`{ "fn": "param", "name": …, "value": … }`) — the one
  address no catalog can give you, since nothing outside the spec names
  it. `value` is absent when the param holds a Field (the expression is
  the value; the `fieldParam` rows that follow are what a knob turns),
  and `schema` for a `fieldParam` is derived from the value's shape plus
  whatever the `param` node declares (`min`, `max`, `description`).
  `exposed` marks the ones an author declared worth turning — a
  wrapper's exposed params and every inline field param — as against a
  standard node's params, which are addressable but mostly wiring.
  `items` params and nodes with no registered schema are omitted; the
  graph's own seed is not a node param and is not in the list. The
  editor builds its knobs from this, so a panel file, a shared link and
  the CLI cannot disagree about what a param is called. From the command
  line: `pcg validate <graph.json> --params` (add `--json` for the same
  list machine-readable), which prints the graph-scoped rows first and
  annotates each with `read by <n> slots: …`, or `read by nothing`.
- `describeGraphAssets(graph)` — the same shape of answer for the OTHER
  free-text surface: every `spawnInstances` in the graph and in every
  subgraph body, in node order, as
  `{ node, assetId, assetAttr?, ids, open }`. `node` is the node id, or
  `"wrapper > inner"` for one inside a body. `ids` is every asset id that
  node can emit, deduplicated in first-occurrence order, each tagged with
  where it came from — `{ from: "assetId" }` for the param, or
  `{ from: "attribute", writtenBy }`, which ALWAYS names the
  `setAttribute` that wrote it, because there is no table entry nobody
  wrote. The point is that an asset id is a promise to a renderer the
  library has never met, so it cannot validate one — but it can tell you
  which promises a graph makes, before it cooks, and without a seed
  having to happen to reach a branch. `open` is the completeness flag and
  the ONLY one: empty means the id set is closed, and a non-empty entry
  (`{ node, type, reason }`) says why the list is a LOWER BOUND. Reported
  OPEN rather than guessed at: an id arriving through promotion,
  transfer, `attributeRemap`, `copyToPoints`, a partition or a wrapper
  boundary; a `setAttribute` whose value is a field, or whose `values`
  the walk cannot read as a string list; and — the case a typo'd
  `assetAttr` actually hits — nothing upstream writing the attribute at
  all, where the entry names the SPAWNER itself rather than some node
  above it. `reason` is written to be printed verbatim. From the command
  line: `pcg assets <graph.json>`.
- `graphParamBindings(params)` / `applyGraphParamTargets(graph, params,
  authored)` / `strandedGraphParamValues(graph)` — the graph-scoped-param
  surface for anything that rebuilds a graph itself rather than going
  through `deserializeGraph`, plus the lint for values that stopped
  tracking their declaration. See docs/authoring.md, "One value, many
  nodes: graph-scoped params".
- `resolveExposedParam(inner, decl)` — build one exposed param for
  `subgraphNode`'s fourth argument. `decl` is
  `{ name, targets, description, default?, min?, max? }`; the schema is
  DERIVED from the targets' registered schemas (identical `type`/`enum`
  required across targets, `acceptsField` ANDed, bounds intersected) and
  the default is the first target's live value unless overridden. Values
  live on the wrapping instance (so instances tune independently and
  cache independently) and are written into the inner graph at cook time
  and restored afterwards, so cooking never modifies the inner graph and
  a graph's serialized bytes never depend on what was cooked — not even a
  cook of another graph sharing the definition, or one that threw. A
  Field on a param that is not field-capable throws at cook time, naming
  the exposed param and the offending inner target. Two exposed params
  binding the same inner slot, or one listing a slot twice, is a hard
  error naming the params and the slot; so is a target that IS the slot
  holding a field expression reading exposed names, since the write and
  the rebuilt expression land on one slot and one of them provably does
  nothing. `targets: []` is legal and means the body's field expressions
  are the param's only route (see `{ fn: "param" }` below); a declaration
  with neither a target nor a reader is refused, listing the names the
  body does read.
- `registerSubgraph(name, spec)` — publish a subgraph under a name so
  serialized graphs can reference it with `ref: { name, hash? }` instead
  of embedding it. `spec` is `{ graph, inputs?, outputs?, params? }` where
  `graph` is a live `Graph` or a `SerializedGraph` and the rest are the
  serialized exposed-pin / exposed-param declarations. The registry stores
  a canonicalized RECIPE (`serializeGraph(deserializeGraph(...))`), never
  a live graph: `subgraphNode` mutates what it wraps, so every reference
  materializes a fresh graph and def through the same
  `deserializeGraph` → `subgraphNode` path an embedded payload takes.
  Hence: a reference and an embedded copy of one recipe cook
  byte-identically (same bytes, same cache decisions, same memo key,
  within one build); two references to one name share no inner graph and
  no caches; and the registry is not a live-update channel (resolution
  happens once at load; duplicate names throw; there is no unregister).
  Returns `{ name, subgraph, hash, meta? }`, frozen.
- `getRegisteredSubgraph(name)` / `hasRegisteredSubgraph(name)` /
  `listSubgraphs()` — lookup (throws listing every registered name),
  membership, and the full list in registration order.
- `subgraphContentHash(payload)` — 16 hex digits. COVERS node ids, types
  and param values, connections, declared outputs, exposed pin mappings,
  and each exposed param's name/targets/default/bounds; a nested `ref`
  contributes the referenced NAME, not its content. EXCLUDES `meta`,
  graph `seed`s and exposed-param `description`s at every level (none can
  change a cooked byte, and hashing `meta` would make a typo fix break
  every pinned graph). Object keys are sorted, so reordering a param
  schema does not move a hash. Stable within one build only.
- `ref.hash` is OPTIONAL: absent means "the registry's current version"
  and upgrades freely; present means the author pinned it and a mismatch
  is a hard error naming both hashes. Neither mode warns; neither cooks a
  near-miss.
- Subgraph nesting must be acyclic and is enforced statically: `Graph.add`
  refuses a node whose def wraps the graph it is added to (directly or
  through a chain), `registerSubgraph` refuses a recipe referencing the
  name being registered, and `deserializeGraph` refuses a name cycle.
  Editing a referenced primitive's inner graph in place and then
  serializing is refused, rather than silently writing the registry's
  content back out.

Mutations keep serialization consistent: `serializeGraph` of a mutated
graph round-trips and cooks identically. Rebuilding via
`deserializeGraph` instead of mutating discards all warm caches.

## Field-expression JSON grammar

A field is a `Field` VALUE and not a text format: in TypeScript it is
what a combinator returns — `mul(perlinNoise({ frequency: 0.05 }), 3)` —
composed before any geometry exists. This grammar is that same object
graph SERIALIZED, one JSON object per combinator, so a saved graph can
carry one: `{ "fn": "mul", "args": [{ "fn": "perlinNoise", "opts": {
"frequency": 0.05 } }, 3] }`. Same fns, same arguments, same column per
element; the only place the library tells the two spellings apart is GPU
eligibility (AUTHORED vs DERIVED spec, below). README.md "Fields" is the
TypeScript side.

AS TEXT — `printFieldSpec(spec)` and `parseFieldText(text)` are a
bidirectional view over the SAME tree. `graphs/basics-filter-by-expression`'s
38-line predicate is
`(length(position()) < 20) * (valueNoise({ frequency: 0.06, seed: { from: "node", variant: 3 }, position: position() }) > 0.4)`.
Text is NEVER saved: it parses to the tree, the tree is the format and is
what every programmatic edit touches (`withInlineParamValue`,
`applyParamPatches`, World patches, editor knobs), so a stored string
would be re-printed by the first edit anyway. The syntax reads like the
TypeScript API: `+ - * /` and `< <= > >= == !=` infix with JS precedence
and minimal parens; `attribute("density")`, `attribute("tangent", 3)`;
`byAttribute("part", { rod: 1 }, 1)`; `component(expr, 0)`;
`ramp(expr, [[4.5, 0.02]])`; `lookup(expr, [0, 0.5, 1])`; a noise takes one object
`perlinNoise({ frequency: 0.05, seed: { from: "node", variant: 0 } })`;
everything else is `name(arg, …)`. `constant(3)` and a bare `3` are
DIFFERENT text because they are different trees — the corpus holds both —
and collapsing them would make the round trip rewrite one into the other.
INPUT-ONLY SUGAR, never printed: `&&`/`||` parse as `mul`/`max` (no
boolean type; comparisons yield 1 and 0), unary `-` folds into a literal
or becomes `sub(0, x)`, and single quotes / trailing commas / redundant
parens are accepted. `P` is NOT sugar for `position()`; the error says so.
Proven rather than asserted: `parseFieldText(printFieldSpec(s))`
deep-equals `s` for every corpus spec, and printing is idempotent.

WHICH PARAMS ACCEPT ONE — 44 of the standard library's 180, across 25
node types, after the rule was swept over every numeric param rather
than applied case by case (it started at 20; only four were refused —
`splineSample.spacing` and `volumeSample.cellSize`/bounds — all on the
allocation clause). A param can
be a field exactly when its value is read PER ELEMENT; everything
settled before the elements are walked cannot be one:

- The column is f32: all 44 are `f32` (27) or `vec3` (17). No `i32`,
  `u32`, `enum`, `bool`, `string` or list param, ever — a field resolves
  per element into a column, and only f32 and its tuples read one. Part
  of it is executable: `acceptsField` on `items`/`numberList`/
  `stringList` is refused at node registration. Same reason a noise's
  `opts.seed` is closed to arbitrary specs — an f32 column rounds a seed
  to 24 bits, and one ULP in a seed is not a rounding error but
  `hashCombine` avalanching to an unrelated u32.
- There must already be elements to evaluate against: the 9 source nodes
  (`meshPrimitive`, `pointGrid`, `pointLine`, `pointScatterInBounds`,
  `pointScatterInWorld`, `valueConstant`, ...) hold 16 `f32`/`vec3`
  params between them and ZERO field-capable ones, because a source
  builds its elements FROM those params.
- Read before the walk stays eager: all 8 `seed` params hash-combine
  into the node's derived seed at cook start, with no element in hand.
- Nothing read ONCE to size a single allocation: `volumeSample.cellSize`
  and its bounds, because that node builds ONE grid — one value, no
  element to read it per. This clause first read "nothing that decides
  how many elements come out", and the C2 sweep proved that wrong:
  `pathResample.spacing` decides exactly that and IS field-capable,
  because the node resamples every polyline on its own arc length, so the
  field resolves per PRIMITIVE — one spacing per path, each path's count
  from its own value. `splineSample.spacing` is the same word in the same
  units and cannot be one — it DOES keep each sample's source primitive,
  but walks the concatenated length from s = 0, so which polyline a
  sample lands on is known only AFTER the step that placed it: the value
  cannot precede the element it would be indexed by. The question is never what the param decides, it
  is whether an element exists to read it per; a global cap on a fielded
  allocation param becomes a post-resolution check. `volumeSample` shows
  both halves in ONE node: `jitter` is a field (read per output centre),
  `cellSize` cannot be (it sizes the grid those centres come from).
- A SYMMETRIC RELATION needs a stated symmetrisation — a REQUIREMENT,
  not an exclusion, and it refuses nothing today. A per-point radius
  makes "A is near B" and "B is near A" two tests, so a relation needs a
  rule for which wins; both nodes that define one use the LARGER of the
  two radii (`selfPrune.minDistance` always has, `filtering.ts:1252`;
  `connectPoints.radius` adopted it on becoming field-capable). A
  per-POINT measurement like `pointNeighborhood.radius` owes nothing
  here. This clause first called such a relation IMPOSSIBLE to field and
  named connectPoints as the case — wrong twice, since selfPrune was
  already doing it. Fielding connectPoints costs MAX_EDGES measured at
  the widest resolved radius, and a partition halo that becomes the
  field's global maximum rather than `radius`.

NON-reasons, both of them plausible: grid cell size (`selfPrune`
resolves the field to a column FIRST and sizes its cells from the
largest resolved claim, and `adjacencyFor` excludes cell size from its
cache key because it changes only how many cells a query touches, never
the answer — a mismatch is slow, never wrong), and deciding how many
elements SURVIVE (`selfPrune.minDistance` decides survival and is a
field; the clause above is about ALLOCATION).

WHAT THE RULE FOUND: when first stated it disagreed with the library on
exactly one param — `pointNeighborhood.radius`, per-point, grid-local and
symmetry-free, so the rule said field and the library said no, for no
stated reason. It is a field now, per point, and neighborhood is
therefore ASYMMETRIC: B within A's radius does not put A within B's, and
that is what a per-point radius means. Caveat carried by every fielded
radius under a partitioned
cook: the halo must be the field's GLOBAL MAXIMUM and the AUTHOR
supplies it inside `bind`, since nothing in `src/runtime/` reads a
node's radius param; underestimating keeps pairs closer than the field
asked for, at the seams only.

A field spec is `{ "fn": <name>, ...args }`. Entries in `args` arrays
may be nested specs, finite numbers, or number arrays (plain values wrap
into `constant`). All 63 fns (`listFieldFns()`):

- Inputs:
  - `{ fn: "constant", value: 1 | [1, 2, 3] }`
  - `{ fn: "attribute", name: "density", tupleSize?: 1 }` (numeric attrs only)
  - `{ fn: "attributeIs", name: "species", value: "pine" }` — the way a
    STRING attribute drives a field, and a PREDICATE, not an accessor: 1
    where the attribute equals the literal, 0 elsewhere, on any domain.
    It never hands back the string-table index, which is insertion-ordered
    and rebuilt by clone/filter/merge, so the same value sits at different
    indices in different cells of one partitioned world. A literal the
    geometry's table does not hold is ALL ZEROS and NOT an error — a cell
    holding no pines legitimately has no `"pine"` to find, so throwing
    would make the answer depend on the partition; the price is that a
    MISSPELLED literal reads as "nothing matches". Structural mistakes do
    still throw: a missing attribute, and a numeric one whose message
    names `eq(attribute(name), value)` as what was meant
  - `{ fn: "byAttribute", name: "part", cases: { "rod": 1, "panel": [1, 0.7, 1] },
    default: 1 }` — the N-way form of `attributeIs`: the case whose KEY
    equals the string attribute's value, or `default` where none does.
    Case values are full argument positions (spec, number, or tuple) and
    broadcast against each other like any combinator's inputs, so the
    result's tuple size is a property of the expression and never of
    which case fired. The `default` is REQUIRED, and that is the point of
    the fn: an unnamed fall-through cannot be searched for, reviewed or
    edited, because it is the absence of an expression rather than one.
    Case keys are NOT validated against the string table and cannot be —
    a key the table does not hold matches nothing and takes the default,
    for the same partition-independence reason `attributeIs` yields
    zeros. So a MISSPELLED key is dead code, not an error. What it buys
    is that the fall-through is explicit and the case set is enumerable
    in one place. Parse-time checks: non-empty `name`, at least one case,
    a present `default`, tuple sizes that broadcast. Duplicate keys are
    NOT checkable — `JSON.parse` collapses them before the grammar runs.
    Every case is evaluated then selected between, as the nested `lerp`s
    it replaces already did; at most one case can fire, so the answer
    does not depend on the order the cases are written in
  - `{ fn: "position" }` — reads P (tuple 3); `{ fn: "index" }` — 0,1,2,...
  - `{ fn: "fraction" }` — normalized index `i / (count - 1)`, spanning
    [0, 1] CLOSED: exactly 0 on the first element and exactly 1 on the
    last, the same convention as `pointLine`'s `includeEnd`. A single
    element gives 0, an empty domain gives nothing. Because the endpoints
    coincide, a periodic function repeats its start value at the last
    element — scale by `(count - 1) / count` for a seam-free loop. Its
    value depends on how many elements share the domain, so it says
    "position along this thing", never "position in the world"
  - `{ fn: "nodeSeed" }` — the cooking node's own seed, `deriveNodeSeed(graph
    seed, node id)`: the same number `randomField` hashes, and the same
    value on every element. Reach for it when an expression needs that
    number, and NOT when a noise must answer the seed box: that half is
    repaired inside `opts.seed` itself, which besides an integer takes the
    tagged `{ "from": "node", "variant": N }` (Noise, below) — no fn, no
    argument position, no calibration constant. It lands in an f32 column,
    so it is a decorrelation source and not an integer to compare. Not in
    `Field.key` (fixed at construction, while the seed arrives at
    evaluation) and it does not need to be — the executor's node memo key
    already carries the node seed, so every node recooks when the graph
    seed moves. BACKGROUND, not instruction: before `opts.seed` took a
    tagged form it was read as a plain number, so the only way in was an
    ARGUMENT position, and graphs folded a bounded per-axis
    `A * (fract(nodeSeed * 2^-32 * K) - W0)` into `opts.position`
    (`A ≈ 32 / opts.frequency`, `K ∈ {1021, 3067, 8191}` one per noise on a
    node, `W0` the fold's value at that graph's default seed, which zeroed
    the offset exactly there and kept a saved graph's bytes). NO graph
    under `graphs/` writes it now — commit `8faf95d` converted all 39
    folds across 25 files, because `W0` is correct for one (graph seed,
    node id) pair and goes stale on a rename, and six of the corpus' 117
    were wrong — but it is still legal grammar, four fixtures in
    `tests/foldCorpus.test.ts` pin the constant-fold against it, and a
    graph saved earlier may hold one. Two hazards outlive it for anything
    still folding a seed into a position: never the unbounded
    `mul(nodeSeed, 1e-6)`, which reaches ~1.3e4 world units and degrades to
    ~73 f32 steps per period at frequency 14; and inside a `forEach` body
    BOTH spellings vary per item, since the body cooks at
    `hashCombine(nodeSeed, hashString("forEach"), itemKey)` — per-item
    variation where that is wanted, and a noise no two groups can agree
    about where it is not. See `docs/authoring.md` "Making a saved noise
    answer the seed box", "The seed-shift idiom" for the fold, and
    `graphs/basics-reseed-a-noise.json`, whose one noise carries the tagged
    seed at `variant: 5`
  - `{ fn: "randomField", key?: 0 | "salt" }` — per-element hash random in [0,1)
  - `{ fn: "param", name: "amplitude", value?: 0.5, min?: 0, max?: 4,
    description?: "..." }` — the value bound to
    that name by the graph's top-level `params` block (above), or by an
    enclosing wrapper's exposed param of the same name
    (every `subgraph` and `forEach` exposed param binds into its body's
    field scope), substituted where the literal would have stood, so the
    field is exactly the field the literal would have built. Uniform over
    the cook: a value that varies per element is an attribute, not a param.
    The optional `value` is the spec's OWN fallback, taken when nothing
    binds the name — so a PLAIN node's expression is tunable without a
    subgraph wrapped around it purely to carry the number, and the same
    spec still works wrapped, because a binder wins over it. A name is
    GRAPH-scoped when the top-level `params` block declares it (one
    declared `cableRadius` drives every slot in the document that names
    it), subgraph-scoped when bound from outside (one exposed `freq` drives
    every body spec that mentions it) and node-scoped when written inline
    (each spec carries its own): a binding belongs to the binder, a literal
    to the expression. A graph-scoped name and an inline `value` for that
    same name is a hard DESERIALIZE error, not a precedence rule — a
    graph-scoped param is the same document as the expression reading it,
    so an always-overridden inline value is dead text and a second
    address for one number, and the message names both sites and both
    fixes (drop the inline `value`, or rename one of the two). The inline
    value is the one binding that survives serialization, being written in
    the spec rather than beside it; a graph-scoped one survives too,
    written in the graph rather than in a wrapper above it. With
    neither, the reference still builds — its key and its GPU kernel need
    only the name — but refuses to evaluate, naming the name and the fix.
    A name may not contain a `.`. Only argument positions can hold one
    (`args` entries, noise `opts.position`); `opts.frequency` and
    `opts.offset` are read as plain numbers, so a tunable frequency
    multiplies `opts.position` instead. `opts.seed` is the one partial
    exception and is not a field either: it takes an integer or the
    tagged `{ from: "node", variant }` (below), whose `variant` alone
    admits an inline `{ fn: "param", name, value }` carrying a whole
    number, substituted like any other and never resolved per element.
    `min`, `max` and `description` describe that inline value the way an
    exposed param's declaration describes its own — the graph stays
    self-describing when a wrapper is flattened into inline values, and a
    panel file refines them rather than owning them. All three are
    optional, require a `value` to describe, and are refused at parse time
    if the bounds are unordered or exclude the value (componentwise for a
    tuple). None of them reaches `Field.key`: they do not change the
    answer, so they must not move a memo key. There is no `step` —
    `ParamSchema` has none
- Elementwise, `args` with exact arity (scalars broadcast; f64 math, f32 storage):
  - 2 args: `add sub mul div min max lt le gt ge eq ne dot cross distance mod rem pow step atan2`
    (comparisons emit 1/0, and `ne` is the exact complement of `eq`;
    `dot` and `distance` reduce tuples to a scalar; `cross` is WIDTH 3
    ONLY on both args and does NOT broadcast scalars; `pow` needs a base
    above 0 — a negative base, `pow(0, 0)` and `pow(x, 0)` for
    non-positive `x` are all NaN, following the `exp2(b * log2(a))`
    identity the GPU implements; `step` is (edge, x) and equals
    `ge(x, edge)`; `mod` is FLOORED — `x - y*floor(x/y)`, so the sign
    follows the DIVISOR and `mod(-1, 8)` is 7, NOT the -1 that JS `%`
    and WGSL `%` give — that -1 is `rem`, below. That is a permanent
    choice made for coordinate
    wrapping/tiling: a truncated remainder mirrors the tile across the
    origin, so a pattern breaks along x=0 and z=0 — the two lines a
    world is most likely to be built around. A zero divisor is NaN on
    both paths;
    `rem` is the TRUNCATED remainder `x - y*trunc(x/y)` and the other
    half of that pair: its sign follows the DIVIDEND, so `rem(-1, 8)`
    is -1 where `mod(-1, 8)` is 7. They AGREE above zero — `rem(9, 8)`
    and `mod(9, 8)` are both 1 — which is what makes picking the wrong
    one silent; a negative divisor swaps them again (`rem(9, -8)` is 1,
    `mod(9, -8)` is -7). `rem` follows the CONVENTION of JS `%`, C's
    `fmod` and WGSL's `%` — sign of the dividend — so use it when
    porting an expression out of a host language, `mod` when tiling.
    It is NOT the same FUNCTION as a true fmod: fmod is exact for any
    operands and gives a zero result the DIVIDEND's sign, where this
    expansion gives +0 (`-8 % 8` is -0 in JS, `rem(-8, 8)` is +0 here).
    Zero divisor NaN on both paths. Both are bit-exact on the GPU by
    the same construction (the CPU rounds the divide, the multiply and
    the subtraction to f32 one at a time, matching the kernel's
    expansion step for step) and both stop being a remainder past
    |x/y| > 2^24, where the quotient can no longer hold an exact
    integer — `rem(1e9, 3)` is 0 here where JS `%` says 1, and `mod`
    does the same with the same divisor, so it is the PAIR's limit and
    not a defect of `rem`. WGSL's `%` is NOT emitted though it means
    the right thing: the spec defines `%` on floats as
    that expansion but the backends it lowers through need not agree —
    a true fmod (MSL, SPIR-V `OpFRem`) stays exact where the expansion
    has already lost the quotient's low bits — so the expansion is
    written out to pin which one the device runs. PORTABILITY only, and
    measured: emitting `%` leaves the reference adapter's parity table
    green, so the form is pinned as emitted WGSL text instead. The NAMES are the
    floored/truncated pair of Ada, Common Lisp, Haskell and Julia;
    `fmod` was rejected as a name for CONTAINING the other one, which
    is how the wrong fn gets reached for;
    `distance` is exactly `length(sub(a, b))` — the CPU rounds the
    difference to f32 BEFORE squaring precisely so the fused and the
    composed spelling cannot drift — and the absolute difference on
    scalars; `atan2` args are [y, x], radians)
  - 1 arg: `abs floor trunc fract sign sqrt exp exp2 log log2 length normalize sin cos tan asin acos atan`
    (trig in radians, elementwise; `trunc` rounds TOWARD ZERO where
    `floor` rounds toward -Infinity — `trunc(-1.5)` is -1, `floor(-1.5)`
    is -2; an exact integer comes back unchanged and `trunc(-0.5)` is
    -0, not +0. `floor` to BIN a coordinate, `trunc` to COUNT whole
    units outward from an origin: only `floor` gives bins of equal
    width across zero, since `trunc` maps both (-1, 0) and (0, 1) onto
    0 and the bin at the origin comes out twice as wide. Emits the WGSL
    `trunc()` builtin, bit-exact; `fract` is `x - floor(x)` and so is
    NON-NEGATIVE for finite input — `fract(-0.25)` is 0.75, exactly
    `mod(x, 1)` — and NaN for a non-finite one; `sign` is
    `(x > 0) - (x < 0)`, which differs from `Math.sign` on two inputs on
    purpose: NaN gives 0 rather than NaN, and -0 gives +0 rather than
    -0. It is what `normalize` already does to a scalar and exists to
    buy the NAME, the precedent `step` set; `exp` is e^x, overflowing to
    Infinity above ~88.7 and underflowing to 0 below ~-103.9, which is
    f32's range and not this implementation's; `exp2` is 2^x and is NOT
    a spelling of `pow(2, x)` — measured hardware implements
    `pow(a, b)` as exactly `exp2(b * log2(a))`, so `pow(2, x)` is
    `exp2` with a logarithm and a multiply in front of it, at `pow`'s
    parity budget of 8 against `exp2`'s 1. `exp2` spans f32's whole
    exponent range: `exp2(128)` is Infinity, `exp2(-150)` is 0 (where
    `exp` gives up at ~88.7 and ~-103.9, the same limits in the wrong
    base), and a whole exponent inside it comes back exact — a
    construction on the CPU side only, since WGSL gives `exp2` a ULP
    tolerance and not an exactness rule, so the device agreeing there
    is measured on the reference adapter, not guaranteed;
    `log` is the NATURAL log, `log(0)` is -Infinity and a negative
    input is NaN, and an arbitrary base is `div(log(x), log(b))` — but
    base two is `log2`, one device instruction where
    `div(log(x), log(2))` is two transcendentals and a division; reach
    for it whenever the question is a count of doublings (which fbm
    octave a frequency belongs to, how many bits a range needs, how
    many halvings a LOD sits from the root). `log2(0)` is -Infinity and
    a negative input is NaN, as `log`. Both
    `exp2` and `log2` emit the WGSL builtin of the same name and
    measure TIGHTER than the base-e pair — 0.50 against `exp`'s 4.12,
    0.65 against `log`'s 0.93 — because the builtin is the instruction
    the hardware has and `exp`/`log` are the scaled compositions built
    on top of it)
  - 3 args: `clamp` (x, lo, hi), `lerp` (a, b, t), `select` (cond, a, b),
    `smoothstep` (edge0, edge1, x — 0 at or below edge0, 1 at or above
    edge1, `t*t*(3-2t)` on the clamped t between, so BOTH ends leave
    flat. The expansion is emitted rather than WGSL's `smoothstep()`
    builtin, whose result is undefined for edge0 >= edge1; a ZERO SPAN
    is guarded the way `remap`'s degenerate input range is, giving the
    step the curve approaches — 1 where x >= edge0. Reach for `ramp`
    when the knees belong anywhere but the ends)
  - 5 args: `remap` (x, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax; unclamped)
- Structure:
  - `{ fn: "vec", args: [x, y, z] }` — 1+ args, concatenates components
  - `{ fn: "component", args: [tupleField], index: 0 }` — extract one component
  - `{ fn: "ramp", args: [scalarField], stops: [[0, 0], [1, 1]] }` —
    piecewise-linear through [position, value] stops, strictly ascending,
    clamped at the ends
  - `{ fn: "lookup", args: [indexField], table: [0.4, 1, -2] }` — the
    table entry at that index, ROUNDED to nearest and CLAMPED into the
    table (every input answers with an entry; no NaN, and no wrap
    option). `mod(i, n)` in front of it wraps an INTEGER index exactly;
    for a FRACTIONAL index it is not a wrap, because the round happens
    AFTER the mod — `mod` lands in [0, n) and the top half-step
    [n - 0.5, n) then rounds to n and clamps back to the LAST entry
    rather than reaching the first (at n = 5, an index in [4.5, 5) reads
    entry 4, not entry 0). Floor the index before the mod if the seam
    matters. Literal finite numbers only, at most 32 of them; the table
    is baked into the GPU kernel as literals, so distinct table VALUES
    specialize as surely as distinct lengths ([1, 2, 3] and [1, 2, 4]
    emit two helpers). A bigger table belongs on the geometry, read with
    `attribute`
- Noise (scalar fields of the sample position; pure function of seed +
  position — the context seed reaches them only through the tagged
  `opts.seed` below):
  - `{ fn: "valueNoise" | "perlinNoise" | "simplexNoise", opts?: {
      seed?: int | { from: "node", variant?: int }, frequency?: number,
      offset?: [x, y, z], position?: spec, normalized?: false } }`
    valueNoise in [0,1); perlin/simplex approx [-1,1]
  - `{ fn: "worleyNoise", opts?: { ...same, output?: "f1" | "f2" | "f2-f1",
      exact?: false } }`
    (distance to nearest/2nd-nearest feature point; f1 in [0, ~1.73);
    `exact: true` widens the cell search until provably exhaustive —
    slower, use when the fast approximation's rare artifacts matter)
  - `{ fn: "fbm", base: "perlinNoise" | "valueNoise" | "simplexNoise" | "worleyNoise",
      opts?: { ...same, octaves?: 4, lacunarity?: 2, gain?: 0.5 } }`
    (sum not renormalized: range grows toward base * (1-gain^octaves)/(1-gain))
  - `normalized: true` (any noise, fbm included) affinely remaps the
    documented raw range to exactly [0, 1]. Raw ranges are
    machine-readable: `NOISE_RAW_RANGES` (per noise type) and
    `noiseOutputRange(field)` (per field instance, fbm-aware).
  - `seed` (any noise, fbm included) is an integer or ONE tagged form,
    `{ "from": "node", "variant": N }`, which derives it as
    `hashCombine(the cooking node's own seed, variant)` — u32 murmur with
    no float in it, hence bit-exact CPU/GPU where a noise interior is only
    budgeted — and is what makes a SAVED noise answer the graph's seed box.
    `variant` stands where the old literal seed stood and picks WHICH draw
    off that node: a node has ONE seed, so two noises on it are one field
    unless their variants differ. Integer, 0..2^24 (above that an f32
    uniform slot no longer holds every integer), default 0. It is also the
    only slot inside `opts` a knob can reach, as an inline
    `{ "fn": "param", "name": "variant", "value": 0 }` carrying a whole
    number — a panel row with a fractional `step` over it is refused,
    because a variant NAMES a draw rather than scaling one. Adopting the
    form RE-ROLLS the noise (no function of graph seed, node id and variant
    is the identity at a seed nobody named), so it is an edit made once and
    deliberately, never a silent upgrade. A noise that must agree across a
    seam keeps its LITERAL: node-seeded, it follows anything that moves
    that node's seed, so under a partitioned `World` it is a per-cell field
    wherever the bind is not seed-invariant —
    `graphs/examples-streamed-terrain.json` pins its density noise for
    exactly that reason and says so.

Nested example — density in [0,1] from remapped 4-octave noise:

```json
{ "fn": "clamp", "args": [
    { "fn": "remap", "args": [
        { "fn": "fbm", "base": "perlinNoise", "opts": { "frequency": 0.03, "octaves": 4 } },
        -1, 1, 0, 1 ] },
    0, 1 ] }
```

In code, both `fieldFromJson(spec)` fields and combinator-composed
fields serialize back via `fieldToJson` — a combinator derives its spec
from its arguments, so since v0.9 a graph holding
`mul(position(), 0.1)` serializes (before v0.9 `serializeGraph` threw
and pointed at `fieldFromJson`). Four cases refuse: a `makeField`
closure (the sanctioned extension point, not a mistake — see
"Hand-authoring a field" below for the trade it makes); any field
composed over one (the absent spec propagates); a
tree deeper than 256 levels — derivation refuses at exactly the depth
`fieldFromJson` parses, so a spec that could not be re-parsed is never
produced and no graph is written that cannot be read back; and an
argument the constructor accepts but the grammar cannot carry (a
fractional `seed`, a non-finite `frequency`/`offset`/`constant`/`ramp`
stop, an fbm `base` outside the built-in factories, `-0` anywhere — the
parser TAKES a `-0` and the spec would hold it, but `JSON.stringify(-0)`
prints `0`, so a reopened graph builds a different field).
`fieldToJson` names the ONE cause that applied and the fix for it — for
an opaque leaf it names that leaf's structural key, so a `makeField`
buried deep in a combinator tree is identified rather than the
constructor that noticed it; for an ungrammatical argument the message
leads with the offending option (e.g. `` `seed` must be an integer ``).
`serializeGraph` prefixes any of them with `node "<id>" param "<key>": `.
Note this is about DESCRIBING a field, not about where it runs: device
eligibility is narrower and additionally requires either an AUTHORED
spec or `acceptDerivedSpecs` (see the GPU section).

Reading the grammar back, for anything that has to SHOW a spec rather
than only evaluate one — a palette, an error message, a diagram, an
agent choosing a fn before it writes one:

- `listFieldFnInfos()` is the grammar's counterpart of `listNodeTypes()`,
  and it is the catalog to read BEFORE writing a field-valued param.
  Same names in the same order as `listFieldFns()`, but each entry is
  `{ fn, keys, usage, description, args?, outputRange? }` instead of a
  bare string: `keys` are the spec keys allowed beside `fn`, `args` names
  the positional arguments (a `…` name marks a repeated position),
  `description` is never empty and covers the edges that bite, and
  `outputRange` is the documented range where one exists. `listFieldFns()`
  is the same list as names only, which is what error messages quote.
  Prefer the Infos form whenever you need the argument NAMES — the specs
  themselves carry positions, not names.
- `specChildEntries(node)` walks one spec node's children WITH each
  position named, which `specChildren` (values only) cannot do: `sub(a, b)`
  is unreadable as two anonymous children, and `byAttribute`'s case keys
  are the whole content of its branches. Order is part of the contract —
  args in order, then `position`, then `variant`, then `cases` in
  insertion order, then `default` — so a renderer can rely on it. The
  names it gives are STRUCTURAL (`args[0]`, never `edge`), because the
  walk sits below the registry; join to `listFieldFnInfos()` and index
  its `args` when you want the registered name.
- `paramNamesOf(spec)` lists every `{ fn: "param", name }` a spec
  references, sorted and deduplicated — the catalog of what
  `fieldFromJson` must be given before that spec can be built. It walks
  the whole tree including `opts.position`, and it READS rather than
  validates, so it is safe to hand raw JSON that has not been checked yet.

### Hand-authoring a field (makeField)

The grammar is ELEMENTWISE — every fn sees one element at a time — and
it is the only field language a FILE can carry. When the computation is
not elementwise (an order statistic, a whole-column reduction) or has no
name in the grammar, `makeField` is the supported way to write the
evaluator yourself. It is a real extension point, not a mistake; the
price is exact and stated at the end of this section.

A `Field` at runtime is three members plus a brand:

```ts
interface Field<N extends number = number> {
  readonly key: string;                 // stable structural identity
  readonly tupleSize: N | undefined;    // components, when statically known
  evaluate(ctx: EvalContext): Column;   // compute the column
}
```

- `EvalContext` = `{ geo, domain, seed }`.
- `Column` = `{ data, tupleSize }`; `data` is a `Float32Array` /
  `Int32Array` / `Uint32Array` of `count * tupleSize` scalars, SoA
  (element `i`, component `k` at `i * tupleSize + k`). Columns may alias
  live attribute storage (`attribute(name)` returns a `subarray`), so
  treat them as read-only and re-evaluate after mutating the geometry.
  Index the COLUMN, not the attribute behind it: an attribute's own
  `data` is `capacity * tupleSize` long and capacity grows by doubling.
- `makeField(key, tupleSize, evaluate)` is the ONLY constructor. It
  stamps the brand `isField` reads. A plain `{ key, tupleSize, evaluate }`
  literal type-checks as a `Field` (the interface does not declare the
  brand) and `isField` still answers false. `isField` is the gate
  everywhere, so such a literal is not quietly mis-cached — it is REFUSED
  by param validation before the graph is built: `add: node
  "setAttribute_0" (type "setAttribute") param "value": expected a finite
  number, got {"key":"impostor()","tupleSize":1}`. The brand is
  enumerable, so `{ ...field }` stays a field; there is nothing to import
  and nothing to stamp by hand.

THE CONTRACT: **equal keys mean interchangeable columns.** `key` is a
structural identity (kind, params, child keys) and TWO caches key on it —
the executor's node cache (hashing a field as `F(<key>)`) and
`evaluateField`'s per-context memo. The library will compute one field
and hand the column to another that shares its key. Every input that can
change the column must be in the key; nothing that cannot should be.
Three helpers exist for that job and are meaningful only here:

- `elementCount(ctx)` — elements in the context's domain, so the output
  column's `data` holds `elementCount(ctx) * tupleSize` scalars. The
  first line of nearly every evaluator, and read per evaluation rather
  than captured: one field instance is evaluated over domains of
  different sizes.
- `keyNum(v)` — a number as key text, `Object.is`-aware: `-0` becomes
  `"-0"` so it never collides with `0` (their columns differ).
- `keyRef(childKey)` — length-prefixed embedding of a child's key. A
  child key is an arbitrary string, so raw concatenation is ambiguous:
  `f("x,y","z")` and `f("x","y,z")` both concatenate to `f(x,y,z)` and
  would share a cache entry; `keyRef` writes `f(3#x,y,1#z)` against
  `f(1#x,3#y,z)`. Every shipped combinator uses it.

Resolve inputs with `evaluateField(child, ctx)`, not
`child.evaluate(ctx)`: it memoizes per context on `key`, so a
sub-expression shared with a sibling is computed once.

Worked example — standardize a field over the domain (mean 0, sd 1),
which the grammar cannot express at any length because mean and
deviation are properties of the whole column. Reads component 0:

```ts
import { elementCount, evaluateField, keyNum, keyRef, makeField } from "pcg-ts";
import type { Column, EvalContext, Field } from "pcg-ts";

function standardize(of: Field, epsilon = 1e-6): Field<1> {
  const key = `standardize(${keyRef(of.key)},${keyNum(epsilon)})`;
  return makeField<1>(key, 1, (ctx: EvalContext): Column => {
    const n = elementCount(ctx);
    const src = evaluateField(of, ctx);
    const out = new Float32Array(n);
    if (n === 0) return { data: out, tupleSize: 1 };
    let sum = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += src.data[i * src.tupleSize];
    const mean = sum / n;
    let sq = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const d = src.data[i * src.tupleSize] - mean;
      sq += d * d;
    }
    const sd = Math.sqrt(sq / n);
    const scale = sd > epsilon ? 1 / sd : 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) out[i] = (src.data[i * src.tupleSize] - mean) * scale;
    return { data: out, tupleSize: 1 };
  });
}

// Drops into any field-capable param; composes with combinators both ways.
const set = g.add(setAttribute, {
  name: "rank", domain: "point", type: "f32", tupleSize: 1,
  value: standardize(component(position(), 0)),
});
```

THE TRADE, and it is the whole cost: a hand-authored field cannot be
DESCRIBED, so it cannot leave the process. `getFieldSpec` returns
`undefined` for one and the absence propagates outward through any
combinator composed over it. Three consequences, one fact:

- `serializeGraph` refuses — no saving, no editor, no corpus fixture.
  The message names the node, the param and the cause: ``node "<id>"
  param "<key>": fieldToJson: this field carries no JSON spec ... It was
  built by makeField ... Rebuild it with grammar constructors``.
- No off-thread cooking: the pool serializes before anything crosses the
  thread — `cook` takes a `SerializedGraph`, and `cookCell` (the backend a
  `World` drives) is handed a live `Graph` and calls `serializeGraph`
  itself.
- No GPU: WGSL is compiled from the spec, so the param evaluates on the
  CPU and counts a `no-spec` fallback.

What it does NOT cost is cooking. In-process a hand-authored field is a
first-class node param — it cooks, caches on its `key`, and is
deterministic on the same terms as everything else.

CHOOSING: grammar (combinator or JSON — they serialize alike) whenever
the graph must be saved, edited, sent to a worker or run on the GPU.
`makeField` when the computation is not elementwise or has no name in
the grammar AND the graph is built in code and cooked in the same
process. If you need both, put the computation in a registered
`standardNode` instead of in a field: a node's params are plain values,
so nothing has to be describable and the graph serializes normally.

## Node types (full schemas: docs/nodes.md, machine-readable: docs/nodes.json)

`listNodeTypes()` entries carry an optional `category` grouping label
(absent when a type declared none); the standard library is fully
categorized: source, sampler, surface, point op, filter, attribute,
value, spawn, io, composite.

- attributeReduce — reduce an attribute across a domain to one detail value (sum/min/max/average/count); unlike promoteAttribute it writes under its own `outName` (so a min and a max can coexist), adds `count`, and SKIPS non-finite values instead of propagating them
- attributeRemap — remap an attribute's range: `range` maps a stated [inMin, inMax] onto [outMin, outMax], `fit` measures the actual finite range first (the only way to normalize, since no param can read a value out of the geometry); NaN stays NaN rather than becoming a valid-looking number
- connectPoints — the only node that turns a point cloud INTO a network: one 2-vertex `polyline` primitive per edge, built over the SAME points, so every point attribute survives and a junction is genuinely ONE point shared by every edge meeting there (degree > 1, which pointsToPath cannot express — it gives each point exactly one group). `mode: "radius"` joins every pair closer than `radius`; `"relativeNeighborhood"` additionally demands that no third point be closer to BOTH endpoints than they are to each other (the lune test), which thins a blob into a road-like net that still CONTAINS a minimum spanning tree — connected wherever the radius reached — while keeping cycles, so it is a network and not a tree. `radius` is a plain number and deliberately NOT field-capable: a per-point radius would make "A is near B" disagree with "B is near A". The test is STRICT (`d < radius`), which is what makes a partitioned cook exact. Optional reporting slots: `degreeAttr` (u32 point, edges touching each point) and `lengthAttr` (f32 PRIMITIVE, each edge's world length); both refuse a name already held under a different shape rather than deleting the column. Edge order is canonical in the POINTS (identity, then position bits, then seed), each edge's FIRST vertex is its lower-keyed endpoint, and any existing topology on the input is REPLACED. **There is no edge domain and none is needed** — see "Networks" below
- copyToPoints — copy a source cloud onto every target point (output = source x target, grouped by target), composing transforms per copy (P/rot/scale fold the target's frame into the source's) and seeds (hashCombine(sourceSeed, targetSeed)). Every SOURCE point attribute rides through unchanged, and `targetNames` is how a copy learns WHICH target it landed on: each named TARGET point attribute arrives as a column keeping the target's type, tuple size and default, every copy in a target's block holding that target's value — which is what lets copies vary by a species tag, an age, or a noise sampled per target instead of being identical in everything but placement. Four kinds of name are refused rather than resolved silently: `P`, `rot`, `scale` and `seed` (composed per copy and already holding the target's contribution, so carrying one would overwrite every copy in a block with the target's own value — copy it to another name on the target with setAttribute and carry that), a name the SOURCE also carries (the two would write the same column and statement order would pick the winner), a name repeated in the list, and a name the target does not have. The approximation to avoid is transferAttribute with mapping `"nearest"` after the copy: it re-derives the correspondence from DISTANCE, so a source point offset from the origin, a large target scale, or targets spaced closer than the source cloud's radius all silently reassign copies — a wrong value rather than an error, where the index correspondence is exact and free inside this node
- dataInput — emit externally injected DataItems (`items` set via graph.setParam; serializes as `items: []`, re-bind live data after deserializing)
- extrudePolygon — SURFACE from a closed footprint: every CLOSED `polyline` primitive is treated as a polygon boundary and swept along a direction into 3-vertex `poly` triangles (walls, floor, roof), which is what turns a computed plot into massing and a boundary loop into a wall. `distance` is field-capable and resolves on the INPUT points, so a per-point value gives a SLOPED top; `direction` is `+y`, a `vector`, or each polygon's own Newell normal. Walls, top cap and bottom cap keep SEPARATE points so the eaves stay a crease, and caps are fan-triangulated from the boundary's first point — exact for a CONVEX plan, and all the topology records. Winding comes from the polygon's Newell normal against the direction, so either winding faces out. Input POINT attributes are copied onto the points that came from them and input PRIMITIVE attributes are gathered onto the triangles; VERTEX attributes are dropped; `normal` and `uv` are reporting slots the node writes. An OPEN polyline is refused by name (fix: pointsToPath with `closed: true`)
- filterByAttribute — keep points where a scalar/string attribute passes a comparison
- filterByBounds — keep points inside/outside an axis-aligned box. `boundary` decides what happens ON a face, and it is the difference between a selection and an OWNERSHIP RULE: `halfOpen` (the default) keeps min <= p < max per axis, so two boxes meeting at a face — one's max is the other's min, the same number — tile space with no gap and no duplicate, which is what makes this the ownership node of a partitioned cook; `inclusive` keeps min <= p <= max and emits a point on a shared face from BOTH boxes. `mode: "outside"` is the exact complement under whichever boundary is active, so inside ∪ outside is always a partition of the input. Infinite bounds are legal, so the unbounded Y of an `"xz"` World column needs no extra param; a NaN coordinate is never inside and lands in `outside`. Bind the box from the UNWIDENED cell (`ctx.min`/`ctx.max`) and the exactness comes from the shared endpoint VALUE — never recover the cell index as `floor(p / cellSize)`, which can name the neighbour when the size is not exactly representable
- filterByDensity — keep points by `density` (threshold or probabilistic)
- filterByExpression — keep points where a field-capable boolean `predicate` is positive; NaN never survives (`v>0||v<0`, not `!==0`), and a tuple>1 predicate is refused rather than broadcast
- filterPrimitivesByAttribute — keep WHOLE PRIMITIVES whose named PRIMITIVE attribute passes a comparison, and one of the two filters in the library that PRESERVE TOPOLOGY: survivors keep their vertices, their vertex and primitive attributes, and the points they share, so a network that goes in comes out a network. It is filterByAttribute one domain up — the same six comparisons, the same numeric/string split, the same scalar-only (tuple 1) rule — and filterPrimitivesByBounds' sibling, differing only in what it asks about a primitive: a value it carries rather than where its vertices lie. Numeric attributes compare against `value`; string attributes against `stringValue` under `eq`/`ne` only, which includes `primtype`, so `primtype eq polyline` is how a mixed geometry is narrowed to its curves. WHERE THE FILTER SITS IS THE POINT: a primitive attribute (connectPoints' `lengthAttr`, a promoted density, anything promoteAttribute lifted onto the primitive domain) can also be read AFTER a sampler has flattened it onto points, because every sampler carries primitive columns down, and filterByAttribute then works — that is how such graphs were written before this node existed; the cost is that the flattening, and everything downstream of it, runs on primitives that were always going to be discarded, so filtering here makes the work that follows proportional to what survives rather than to what was proposed. `unreferencedPoints: "keep"` (the default) leaves the point domain UNTOUCHED — same points, same indices, same attributes, same identities — while `"drop"` removes every point no surviving primitive references and renumbers the topology onto what remains. DETERMINISM: the test reads ONE primitive's own value and nothing else — not its index, not its neighbours, not how many primitives there are — so the survivors and their order are the input's however the cook was partitioned, and no index column is emitted for a per-partition number to leak into a fingerprint; a polyline whose points span two cells is emitted whole by the single cell that owns its first vertex (filterPrimitivesByBounds' `vertex: "first"` + `halfOpen` ownership rule), so it is tested exactly once and with its complete value. A name that lives on the POINT domain instead is refused with the fix (promoteAttribute onto the primitive domain, or filterByAttribute if points really are what you want), and filterByAttribute carries the mirror-image message. A geometry with no primitives is an empty result, not an error
- filterPrimitivesByBounds — keep or drop WHOLE PRIMITIVES by testing their vertices against an axis-aligned box, and one of the two filters in the library that PRESERVE TOPOLOGY (filterPrimitivesByAttribute, which tests a value a primitive carries rather than where its vertices lie, is the other): survivors keep their vertices, their vertex and primitive attributes, and the points they share, so a network that goes in comes out a network. Every point filter (filterByDensity, filterByBounds, filterByAttribute, filterByExpression, selfPrune) rebuilds the point domain from the survivors and the primitives go with it; this one filters the PRIMITIVE domain, and that single difference is the whole node. It exists to complete the partitioned network cook, whose last step had NO node before it: clip the cloud to the WIDENED rectangle with filterByBounds (`halfOpen`), run connectPoints, then run THIS on the UNWIDENED rectangle with `vertex: "first"` and the same `halfOpen` boundary — so the recipe is a serializable graph rather than a TypeScript script. `vertex` decides what "in the box" means, and its four values split into two kinds: `first` (default) and `last` read exactly ONE vertex, which is what makes them OWNERSHIP rules — every primitive has exactly one of each, so exactly one box of a tiling claims it — while `all` (every vertex inside) and `any` (at least one inside) are SELECTIONS and do NOT tile: `any` claims a straddling primitive from every box it reaches, `all` from none of them, so a partitioned cook using either double-counts or loses edges at every seam. Use `all`+`inside` for "roads entirely inside the park", `any`+`outside` for "delete every road touching the lake". connectPoints emits each edge's lower-keyed endpoint FIRST, so `vertex: "first"` makes this node's owner and that node's canonical edge order the same choice by construction; for a polyline from any OTHER source (pointsToPath, pathResample, createPolyline) the first vertex is simply the path's START, so the tiling is still exact but the owner is the cell holding the start and that one cell emits the WHOLE path however far it runs. `boundary` is filterByBounds' rule with the same meaning and the same reason to prefer `halfOpen` wherever ownership matters; `mode: "outside"` is the exact complement of `inside` under whichever vertex rule and boundary are active. `unreferencedPoints: "keep"` (the default) leaves the point domain UNTOUCHED — same points, same indices, same attributes, same identities, so a partition cell keeps its halo points as isolated leftovers — while `"drop"` removes every point no surviving primitive references and renumbers the topology onto what remains in ascending input order (note it also drops points that never had a primitive, so a cloud carrying both a network and unrelated scatter loses the scatter). A geometry with no primitives is an empty result, not an error — a cell too sparse to make an edge is a legitimate silent case. Handles any primitive kind, polylines and polys alike: it reads vertices, never `primtype`
- jitterPoints — deterministic random offset per point (field-capable amount)
