- mergePoints — concatenate point clouds (multi input), union of attributes; TOPOLOGY IS NOT CARRIED, so a network or a mesh arrives and leaves as a bare cloud — `mergePrimitives` is the twin that keeps it
- mergePrimitives — concatenate whole geometries (multi input) KEEPING TOPOLOGY: points, vertices and primitives are all appended and each input's vertex/primitive references renumbered, so an authored path joined to a generated network stays one network. Point, vertex and primitive domains each carry the union of that domain's attributes (missing ones default-fill over that input's range). `primtype` is special-cased because it is a type tag rather than a value: each input's primitives keep their own tag, and an input carrying no primtype column contributes an EMPTY tag rather than inheriting another input's. Mixed primitive kinds are allowed — every consumer selects what it understands. An input with no topology contributes points only; the detail domain is not carried. Point identity (position bits + `seed`) is copied verbatim, so two inputs holding the same position and seed are one point to every identity-keyed decision
- meshPrimitive — SOURCE of triangle-mesh geometry in-graph: a subdivided `plane` (orientation xz/xy/yz, normal along the positive third axis) or a `box` (six faces, per-face points so uv seams are exact); emits P, uv and `poly` primitives. This is the only way to make mesh geometry from JSON — dataInput carries nothing through serialization — so it is what feeds surfaceSample and transferAttribute raycast/uv. It does NOT feed splineSample, which reads `polyline` primitives and skips every other primitive type; the in-graph source of a polyline is pointsToPath (see "Paths")
- orientAlongVector — write `rot` quaternions so a local axis (default `+z`) follows a field-capable direction (e.g. a tangent/normal attribute), `up` hint fixes roll; zero directions keep their rot
- partitionByAttribute — split into per-value point clouds, tagged `name=value`
- pathResample — resample every polyline at even arc-length steps, per path rather than across all of them, and emit a PATH (topology survives, closure survives); `mode: "count"` fixes the sample count per path, `"spacing"` fixes the world-unit step. The points are NEW, so the input's POINT attributes are gone; its PRIMITIVE attributes survive in BOTH directions — every attribute of the polyline a sample came from lands on that sample, and each output polyline keeps the attributes of the input polyline it replaces (output primitive i resamples input polyline i and nothing else), so a resampled road comes back still a road rather than a nameless polyline. `primtype` is never carried and there is no opt-out; a carried name that collides with one this node writes (P, tangent, curveU, seed, ...) is REFUSED with an error naming the node, the attribute, both shapes and the fix
- pointGrid — regular grid of points
- pointLine — evenly spaced points on a segment; `includeEnd` (default true) samples the closed range [start, end], false samples the half-open [start, end) so a sweep that wraps has no duplicate seam
- pointNeighborhood — per-point neighbour statistics from the shared uniform grid: a count within `radius`, and optionally the average of another attribute over those neighbours; `maxCount` keeps the NEAREST N (ties to lower index) and accumulation is always in ascending point index, so a capped average is bit-stable; a point with no neighbours averages to its OWN value, so differences like `P - nbrP` are exactly zero for isolates
- pointScatterInBounds — uniform random points in a box. Positions are computed as a function OF `boundsMin`/`boundsMax`, so widening the box to form a halo MOVES EVERY POINT and reproduces nothing a neighbour saw; reach for pointScatterInWorld whenever a region has to survive being queried twice at two sizes
- pointScatterInWorld — world-ANCHORED source, and the only one. Points live on an INFINITE lattice; a point's position and per-point `seed` are a pure function of (`seed`, `latticeMode`, `cellSize`) plus its own lattice cell and index, and NEVER of the window — `boundsMin`/`boundsMax` only choose which lattice cells to visit and clip the result, half-open, so abutting windows partition the world. Three consequences that no other source can offer: a halo is just a WIDER QUERY (nothing is fetched from a sibling cell, which need never have cooked), a region cooked whole and the same region cooked in pieces agree byte for byte, and two cells on a boundary agree about what is there. Expected population is exactly `density * area` in `latticeMode: "xz"` (a 2D XZ lattice, every point at `height`, Y bounds ignored) or `density * volume` in `"xyz"`, so a count is predictable without cooking; raising `density` only ADDS points. `cellSize` is THIS NODE'S OWN lattice — the patch the count is quantized over, controlling clumping and not population — and must be set from the content's scale, never from a World level's `cellSize` (tying them makes the world a function of the runtime's partitioning). Emission order is by lattice cell (Z outer, then Y, then X) then index, so two windows list their shared points in the same relative order. **It ignores the graph seed** — the one exception to the seed chain; see "Key invariants and contracts"
- pointsToPath — the only node that turns a point cloud INTO a path, so the only way to start one in a serialized graph: builds `polyline` primitives over the SAME points, so every point attribute survives; `closed` appends the structural trailing vertex, `groupAttr` splits the cloud into one path per id, `orderAttr` orders each path (ties to the lower point index). Every point lands in exactly ONE group, so a point here has at most two neighbours and the result can never BRANCH — that is a limit of this node, not of the representation; reach for connectPoints when you want a network
- projectToPlane — orthogonal projection of points onto a plane
- promoteAttribute — move an attribute between domains (first/average/sum/min/max)
- removeAttribute — delete named attributes from a domain (`strict` errors on a missing name); refuses to delete point `P`
- sampleNearestPoint — look up the nearest point of a second `source` cloud per point: distance, source index, and optionally copy one of its attributes; misses report distance Infinity / index -1 and leave a copied attribute at its prior value
- selfPrune — greedy minimum-distance thinning (lowest index wins)
- setAttribute — create/overwrite an attribute from a field-capable value; `type: "string"` picks per element from a `values` list by numeric selector (floor+clamp, total) or writes a constant `stringValue`; optional `seed` param folds into the field evaluation (0 = node seed unchanged)
- setBounds — stamp boundsMin/boundsMax on every point
- spawnInstances — terminal: points to render-agnostic instance batches (4x4 column-major transforms, plus optional named per-instance attribute channels, the reserved `color` among them); `assetAttr` names a string attribute for per-point asset ids (empty entries fall back to `assetId`). NEITHER IS CHECKED, and cannot be: an asset id is a free string whose real set belongs to the renderer, so a misspelled or invented one cooks, validates and reports its instance count, then draws as whatever that renderer does with a name it does not know (for a viewer of arbitrary graphs, a stand-in shape rather than an error). `pcg assets <graph.json>` lists every id a graph can emit — this param and the `assetAttr` tables together, across every branch rather than the one a seed reached, and reporting a set it cannot determine as OPEN instead of guessing. Check that list against your renderer; one batch per asset in ascending first-occurrence point order, instances within a batch in ascending point order. `colorAttr` (default `""`) names an f32 point attribute with tupleSize >= 3 whose components 0/1/2 become the instance's RGB — this is how instances of ONE asset id vary in appearance (age, health, season, hue drift) without splitting into more assets. ALPHA IS DROPPED: both three adapters take RGB, so the standard f32x4 `color`'s fourth component has nowhere to go. It is OPT-IN and nothing is sniffed: every cloud in this library already carries `color` at [1,1,1,1], so its presence states no intent, and writing an all-white instance-colour buffer would flip three's program variant (`instanceColor !== null` forces the `vColor` varying and a shader recompile) for zero pixels changed — a value-scan to auto-enable would be O(n) per cook AND make the shader variant data-dependent, which is worse. ACCEPTED COST, stated rather than hidden: an author who writes `setAttribute("color", ...)` and never names it here gets silence, not a warning. Any colour-shaped attribute works (`color`, or a `tint`/`speciesColor` you wrote). A missing attribute, or one that is not f32 with tupleSize >= 3, is an error listing the point attributes that WOULD fit and two fixes. `instanceAttrs` (stringList, default `[]`) carries ANY OTHER point attributes across as NAMED per-instance channels, in the order given: each becomes `batch.attributes[<the attribute's own name>]` — no renaming, so the name in the graph and the name the host binds are the same string. This is the whole per-instance ABI between a graph and its host. The field grammar has no time input ON PURPOSE — a graph settles STRUCTURE and the host animates it — so anything the host must drive per instance at runtime (a phase offset, a stable id, a species index, an RGBA tint, a wind stiffness) has to leave the graph on this list; before it existed only transforms and RGB could cross, and a host had to re-derive the rest from a position, which stopped agreeing with the graph that authored it. DTYPE AND TUPLE SIZE ARE PRESERVED from the point attribute, never widened to f32: f32 has a 24-bit mantissa, so a u32 id past 2^24 (16777216) lands on its neighbour and two instances become one to a host keying on it, and nothing downstream wants the widening anyway (`THREE.InstancedBufferAttribute` takes any typed array). A channel column is tightly packed, `count * tupleSize` elements, instance k at `k * tupleSize`; ITEM SIZE IS NOT CARRIED — recover it as `column.length / count`, so there is no second place for it to be wrong. ORDER IS THE INVARIANT: `attributes[name][k]` and `transforms[k]` are the SAME instance, written in one loop from one source index, so no second traversal exists to fall out of step. `InstanceBatch.colors` is SUGAR for the reserved `"color"` entry of that same record, not a sibling of it — on a batch this library builds it is an accessor returning `attributes["color"]`, one buffer under two spellings, kept so consumers written against the older shape keep working (`instanceAttributesOf(batch)` normalizes either spelling, including a hand-built batch that set a plain `colors` and no `attributes`, and THROWS if a batch carries two different colour buffers — enumerate channels through it rather than reading `.attributes` directly). That is exactly why `instanceAttrs` REFUSES `"color"`: a renderer binds instance colour structurally (three's `InstancedMesh.instanceColor`, a mesh property that flips the shader variant, not a geometry attribute), so a generic channel of that name would be uploaded twice and mean two things — `colorAttr` is its route, and to carry RGBA (which colorAttr's alpha drop cannot) copy the attribute to another name upstream and name THAT here. FIVE things error, each naming the offending entry and the way out, in the order they are checked: an EMPTY name; the same name listed TWICE; the reserved name `"color"` — checked BEFORE the lookup, so it reports as reserved even when no such attribute exists; an attribute MISSING from the point domain (the message lists the point attributes that could become channels); and a `string` attribute (its column is indices into a per-attribute string table that does not travel with it, so a renderer would receive integers that mean nothing — use `assetAttr` for per-point asset ids, or encode the choice as u32/i32 upstream). All five are raised by `buildInstanceBatches`, which is what prefixes them, so grep for the PARAM name rather than the node type. `[]` (the default) carries nothing and allocates nothing, and `batch.attributes` is then ABSENT, exactly as `colors` is absent when no colour was asked for. NOT DEVICE-*PRODUCED* TODAY, WHICH IS NARROWER THAN "CPU-ONLY" AND IS ROUTINELY MISREAD: a spawn naming any channel is REJECTED BY THE DEVICE RUN PLANNER (reason `run-plan-failed`) and the whole terminal falls back to the CPU spawner (see the device-resident instancing section). That is a gate on PRODUCTION ONLY and it says nothing about the other two things a reader assumes it says. (1) RENDERING a channel under a `WebGPURenderer` IS SUPPORTED: `toInstancedMeshes` binds every non-reserved channel as an `InstancedBufferAttribute` of its own name, imports only `three` and branches on nothing renderer-shaped, so a WebGPU material reads it exactly as a WebGL one does — that is the whole supported path for per-instance data in a shader. The library ships the DATA, not the shader: nothing here imports `three/tsl`, and `normalized`/`gpuType` are left at three's defaults, so DECLARING the attribute (TSL `attribute()`, a `ShaderMaterial`, an `onBeforeCompile` patch) and the shader-side type of an integer channel are the HOST'S. The one WebGPU refusal is the DEVICE-RESIDENT adapter, which binds only the instance matrix and the reserved colour. (2) COOKING IS NOT PINNED TO THE MAIN THREAD: `pcg-ts/worker` cooks off-thread and `EncodedInstanceBatch.attributes` carries EVERY named channel (colour included — `colors` is an accessor over the reserved entry and has no wire form of its own), each column on the structured-clone TRANSFER LIST, so batches arrive as buffer ownership rather than as a copy. The worker pays one `slice()` per column on its own thread (cook arrays alias live memo caches and must not be detached); the main thread pays nothing. "CPU" here means NOT-THE-GPU-DEVICE, never on-your-frame. BUDGET: at most 1048576 instances PER COOK (one per input point; 64 MiB of matrices), checked before allocation, so a runaway density is a diagnostic naming the count and the fix instead of an allocation failure. Per COOK, never per world — a global "instances alive" ceiling would depend on which cells happen to be resident and so be order-dependent, which the determinism invariant forbids; a streamed world may legitimately hold many times the budget across its resident cells
- splineSample — arc-length sampling along polyline primitives, treating every polyline of the input as ONE concatenated curve (emits tangent, curveU); its in-graph source is pointsToPath or pathResample, and its own output is a plain point CLOUD, no longer a path. Each sample ALSO carries every attribute of the polyline PRIMITIVE it landed on, even though the polylines are measured as one concatenated curve — a sample exactly on a join between two polylines takes the LATER one's values. `primtype` is never carried and there is no opt-out; a collision with a name this node writes is REFUSED, naming the fix
- subgraph — composite node wrapping an inner graph; create with `subgraphNode(inner, inputs, outputs, params)` (pins AND params are per-instance), inspect with `getSubgraphSpec` / `describeSubgraphPins` / `describeSubgraphParams`, serializes recursively as `subgraph` or by name as `ref`. Its two loop siblings `forEach` (`forEachNode`) and `repeatUntil` (`repeatUntilNode`), both described above, carry the SAME payload under their own `type` — the wrapper kind lives in `type` and nowhere else — and a `repeatUntil` node's `params` additionally hold the loop's own `maxRounds` and `settleAttr`, which no body exposes and every instance has
- surfaceSample — area-weighted scatter on a triangle mesh with density acceptance (emits normal); each sample also carries every attribute of its own triangle's PRIMITIVE, so a per-face value written upstream survives the sampling instead of dying at it (`primtype` excepted, no opt-out, collisions refused)
- sweepProfile — SURFACE from a curve: a cross-section (`circle` / `square` / `ribbon`) is placed on EVERY POINT of every polyline primitive and consecutive placements are stitched into 3-vertex `poly` triangles, so a path finally becomes a skin rather than a run of instanced cylinders (pathSegments is still the right node for a chain of DISCRETE links). THE PATH IS NOT RESAMPLED — one ring per input point, which is why the field-capable `radius`/`width`/`roll`/`up` resolve exactly at the ring instead of being averaged across a segment; run pathResample first for a finer surface. `frame` (`upHint` / `curveFrame` / `rot`) fixes only the ROLL — the ring's plane always comes from the path, so the node computes no frame of its own and adds no non-locality. `joint: "miter"` stretches the ring by 1/cos(half the turn) so the section keeps its radius through a bend, degrading to the unstretched section past `miterLimit`. Closed paths share their first and last ring (so `u` wraps across that one band); `caps` applies only to an OPEN path with a CLOSED profile. Input POINT attributes are copied (not interpolated) around each ring and input PRIMITIVE attributes are gathered onto the triangles; VERTEX attributes are dropped; `normal` and `uv` are reporting slots the node writes, with `u` as normalized arc length matching `curveU`
- transferAttribute — transfer an attribute from a `source` geometry onto the input's points; `mapping`: "nearest" (closest source point in 3D, never misses), "uv" (destination point-domain UVs located in the source triangulation's UV space; source UVs read from the vertex domain when present — seam-correct — else point), "raycast" (forward-only ray per point: `direction` or per-point `directionAttr`, nearest hit, optional `maxDistance`). uv/raycast need a triangle source; f32 interpolates barycentrically, i32/u32/bool/string take the dominant corner (largest weight, ties → first corner); shared-edge/equal-distance ties → lowest source primitive index; misses keep the prior value (attribute default if new), count reportable via `missCountAttr` (u32 detail) and reportable PER POINT via `hitAttr` (bool point, tuple 1, empty = don't write): 1 = this point found a source and received a value, 0 = it missed and kept its prior one. Polarity is the HIT, the inverse of what `missCountAttr` counts. Every point is written, so the column is never stale — `mapping: "nearest"` leaves it all 1 (nothing can miss), a source with nothing to search leaves it all 0. Must differ from `name`. Feed it to filterByAttribute (comparison "eq", value 1) to keep only the points that landed, then removeAttribute to clean up — one ray decides both the move and the discard, which is what `place/drop-to-surface` does in three nodes with no second raycast. `attrDomain` picks the SOURCE domain: "point" (the default, and the only one "nearest" accepts), "vertex" (per-corner, seam-accurate), or "primitive" — one value for the whole triangle, never interpolated whatever its type, so a per-face id, material tag or width arrives bit-exact (`w0·v + w1·v + w2·v != v` in floating point, so blending a constant would return a value nobody wrote). Two refusals worth knowing before you plan around them: "nearest" + "primitive" is REFUSED because that mapping searches source POINTS and a per-primitive value sits on none — promoteAttribute it primitive→point on the source ("max"/"first") and transfer with attrDomain "point", which the error states — and NEITHER uv nor raycast can ever reach a polyline network however you set attrDomain, since both need 3-vertex "poly" triangles and connectPoints/pointsToPath produce none. Points being SAMPLED off a network need none of this: the samplers already carry the value (see "Networks"). Grid acceleration is result-neutral; epsilon policy exported (TRANSFER_BARY_EPS, TRANSFER_AREA_EPS, TRANSFER_DET_EPS, TRANSFER_BOX_PAD_REL)
- transformPoints — per-point translate/rotate/scale, composing with rot/scale attrs (field-capable)
- valueConstant — emit a constant number as a value item
- volumeSample — jittered grid fill of a box or of the input geometry's bounds
- writeTangents — write a unit `tangent` onto a path's OWN points (points, attributes and topology all pass through untouched), for paths that were never spline-sampled; the tangent is the normalized central difference between neighbours along the path and wraps on a closed one, so orientAlongVector has something to read

## Paths and networks (polyline topology)

A path is not a point type and not an attribute. It is TOPOLOGY laid over
points that already exist: `polyline` primitives whose vertices reference
point indices, sitting alongside the usual point domain. The points keep
every attribute they had; the path is the statement that they are visited
in an order. A NETWORK is the same representation with the branching
allowed: many 2-vertex polylines over one shared point set, so a point can
sit on several of them. `pointsToPath` starts a path, `connectPoints`
starts a network; see "Networks" below.

- **Producing one.** `pointsToPath` is the only node that turns a point
  cloud INTO a path, so it is the only way to start one in a serialized
  graph — it builds polylines over the SAME points it is given, so
  nothing written upstream is lost. The `shape/path-loop` and `shape/path-meander`
  primitives are the ready-made sources built on it. In TypeScript,
  `createPolyline` and (with the three adapter) `fromCurve` do the same
  job; a JSON author cannot call either, which is why `pointsToPath`
  exists. `pathResample` and `place/along-curve` take a path and emit a
  path, so they extend a chain rather than start one.
- **Closure is structural.** A closed path is one whose last vertex
  references the path's first point. There is NO `closed` attribute: do
  not write one, do not look for one, and do not test closure by
  comparing positions. `pointsToPath`'s `closed` param appends that
  trailing vertex and writes nothing else; every consumer detects closure
  the same way. A closed path needs at least 3 points.
- **Order is a contract.** Within a path the points are visited in
  ascending point index — the order they arrived on the node's input —
  unless `orderAttr` names a numeric point attribute to sort by
  ascending, and ties in that key ALWAYS break to the lower point index.
  There is no sort-stability question and no arrival-order dependence.
  `groupAttr` splits one cloud into one path per distinct (whole-number)
  group id, emitted in ascending id.
- **A path that goes through a filter STOPS being a path** (and a network
  stops being a network — same mechanism, same silence). Every filter
  node that can REMOVE points routes through `gatherPoints`, which
  rebuilds the point domain from the survivors and drops topology with
  it; `mergePoints` and `partitionByAttribute` drop it too. Exactly three
  filters are exempt, for two unrelated reasons: `projectToPlane` moves
  points without removing any, and `filterPrimitivesByBounds` and
  `filterPrimitivesByAttribute` remove whole PRIMITIVES rather than
  points — the two nodes whose subject is the topology instead of its
  casualty (see "Networks"). It is CAN
  remove, not did: `filterByAttribute` drops topology even when its
  predicate keeps every point. And the node's category decides nothing —
  all three exemptions are categorised `filter`, while
  `partitionByAttribute` is categorised `attribute` and drops. Nothing
  warns at the point of loss — it is silent there, and surfaces later as
  a path consumer reporting that it found no polylines. So: filter
  FIRST, then `pointsToPath`, and put
  every path op (`pathResample`, `writeTangents`, `splineSample`,
  `place/along-curve`, `write/orient-along-path`,
  `filter/by-distance-to-curve` on its `curve` pin) after the last
  filter, never before it.
- **Consuming one.** `splineSample` treats every polyline of its input as
  one concatenated curve and emits a plain point CLOUD (topology ends
  there); `pathResample` measures each path on its own length and emits a
  path. `writeTangents` and `write/orient-along-path` write onto a path's
  own points and hand the path back unchanged — that is the only way to
  orient points that carry meaning, since a sampler's output points are
  new ones.
- **A sampler loses POINT attributes and keeps PRIMITIVE ones.** The two
  halves are asymmetric on purpose and both are load-bearing. The points
  are new, so nothing the input's points carried survives `splineSample`,
  `pathResample`, `place/along-curve` or `surfaceSample` — but every one
  of them carries the SOURCE PRIMITIVE's attributes onto each sample,
  automatically, because a sample inherits the primitive it was taken
  from. That is what puts a road's `roadWidth` on the lamps standing on
  it. `primtype` is the sole exclusion (a type tag, not a value); there
  is no opt-out param, since an author who wrote the value must get it
  without knowing a knob exists; and NO `sourcePrimitive` index column
  ships alongside, because primitive numbering is per-partition and a
  shipped index would break split-equals-whole. A carried name colliding
  with one the node writes itself is REFUSED, naming node, attribute,
  both shapes and the fix — never merged, renamed or silently dropped.
  Accepted cost, so it is not filed as a bug: every upstream primitive
  attribute is now part of a sampler's output contract, so an unrelated
  `lengthAttr` widens the samples too. Bounded (only `connectPoints` and
  `promoteAttribute` make primitive columns), and better than losing the
  value in silence.

## Networks (the primitive domain IS the edge domain)

The obvious question — "how do I put a value on an EDGE?" — has an answer
that is not obvious: **there is no edge domain, and none is needed.** A
2-vertex `polyline` over shared points already IS an edge, so an edge is a
`primitive`, and every per-edge value is an ordinary primitive attribute
written by the nodes that already ship. Nothing about this was added for
networks; `connectPoints` only made the existing representation reachable
from JSON.

The five moves, which are the whole vocabulary:

- **point → edge:** `promoteAttribute` `from: "point"`, `to: "primitive"`.
  `mode: "min"` gives a road the width of its WEAKER end (the conservative
  choice, and the usual one); `"first"` carries a categorical across
  (the lower-keyed endpoint's value, since that is each edge's first
  vertex); `"average"` and `"sum"` also work but are cell-local under a
  World, like every aggregate.
- **on the edge:** `setAttribute` with `domain: "primitive"`. Its field
  sees the primitive domain, so `{"fn": "attribute", "name": "..."}` reads
  a promoted per-edge value and `remap`/`ramp` shape it.
- **edge → junction:** `promoteAttribute` `from: "primitive"`, `to:
  "point"`, `mode: "max"` — every point learns the largest value among the
  edges that touch it, which is how a junction gets sized by the widest
  road reaching it.
- **degree without arithmetic:** `connectPoints`' `degreeAttr` writes it
  directly (u32, point), so a dead end is `degree == 1` and a junction
  `degree >= 3`, both reachable with `filterByAttribute`. `lengthAttr`
  does the same for per-edge length (f32, primitive).
- **edge → the points sampled off it:** nothing to author. Every sampler
  that reads a polyline carries the source primitive's attributes onto
  the points it emits (`splineSample`, `pathResample`,
  `place/along-curve`; `surfaceSample` for triangles), so a lamp placed
  along a road arrives already carrying that road's `roadWidth` and
  `districtKind`. Distinct from move 3: that one aggregates with `max`
  across every edge meeting a junction, this one is exact, because a
  sample sits on exactly one primitive. See "Paths and networks" for the
  exclusions and the refusal rule.

`graphs/pipeline-5-roads.json` runs all five in order
(`roadWeight` → `roadNet` → `roadClass`/`roadKind` → `roadWidth` →
`roadJunction`), and `place/along-curve` then walks the whole net at once,
each edge measured on its own length — its `roadPosts` emits 42 lamps,
each carrying the `roadLength`, `roadWeight`, `districtKind` and
`roadWidth` of the one road it stands on.

**Seeing a per-edge value.** `pcg cook`'s one-line summary lists POINT
attributes only, so an edge attribute is invisible there; `pcg inspect
--node <id> --pin <pin>` prints every domain. `pcg render --attr <name>`
reads BOTH colorable domains and they never compete for one mark — the
point column colors the circles, the primitive column colors the paths —
so a road network carrying `roadWidth` on its roads AND its junctions
colors both, and a value living only on the primitives is visible instead
of unreachable. Points of a geometry that holds the name only on its
primitives keep the flat default color (a junction of three roads has
three candidate values; inventing one would be a picture of nothing in
the data). `--attr-domain point|primitive` narrows the lookup, which
matters because the scalar ramp normalizes over every domain read — one
legend would otherwise span both ranges. Strings color categorically on
either domain. Every render report names the domain the color came from.
`vertex` and `detail` are refused: neither draws a mark of its own.

**A point-removing op destroys a network, exactly as it destroys a path.**
This is the trap that costs the most time, because the network survives
`pcg validate` and cooks without error — it just quietly becomes a cloud
again. `filterByBounds` placed AFTER `connectPoints` is the specific
mistake: clipping a net to a rectangle looks like trimming and is actually
demolition. Two fixes, and only these two:

1. **Clip before connecting.** Every filter goes upstream of
   `connectPoints`, the same "filter first, build the topology after" rule
   paths already carry.
2. **When the clip is a partition boundary, express ownership on the
   lower-keyed ENDPOINT instead of on the points.** Widen the cell's
   rectangle by `radius`, clip the cloud to it with `filterByBounds`
   (`halfOpen`) BEFORE `connectPoints`, then run
   `filterPrimitivesByBounds` on the UNWIDENED rectangle with
   `vertex: "first"` and the same `halfOpen` boundary. That last step is
   a primitive-domain decision — it trims the topology rather than
   dropping it — and it IS a node, so the whole recipe is a serializable
   graph: `filterByBounds(widened, halfOpen)` → `connectPoints` →
   `filterPrimitivesByBounds(unwidened, first, halfOpen)`. Each edge's
   first vertex is its lower-keyed endpoint, so exactly one cell claims
   each edge and the cells tile the network with no duplicate and no
   gap. `vertex: "all"` or `"any"` does NOT tile — see the node's roster
   entry. The runnable JSON and the exactness argument are in
   `docs/authoring.md`, "Owning primitives instead of destroying them".

## Primitive library (full catalog: docs/primitives.md, machine-readable: docs/primitives.json)

34 named subgraphs — the vocabulary a graph is written IN. **They
register on import of their own subpath**, so nothing resolves until
something imports it; `import "pcg-ts"` deliberately does not:

```ts
import "pcg-ts/primitives";
```

The `pcg` CLI imports it, so `pcg run <name>` works with no graph file.
Reference one from JSON with `{"type":"subgraph","ref":{"name":"..."},
"params":{...}}`; read `listSubgraphs()` at runtime for the live set.

Names are `<family>/<kebab-case>` over a CLOSED set of seven families,
and the family is a promise about the pin shape:

- shape (6) — a point set from nothing, built at unit size and placed by
  a trailing transform: ring, spiral, disc, sphere-points, and the two
  that carry polyline topology instead of a loose cloud — path-loop,
  path-meander
- fill (4) — turn a region into a distribution: scatter-even (minimum
  spacing), scatter-by-density (noise clumps), scatter-clustered,
  volume-by-noise (carved 3D volumes)
- transform (3) — change P, keep the count: displace-by-noise,
  snap-to-grid, relax-spacing
- compose (2) — combine two clouds: merge-tagged, scatter-copies
- filter (6) — remove points, never move one, never leave a column
  behind: thin-by-density, mask-by-noise, inside-radius, by-distance-to,
  by-neighbor-count, by-distance-to-curve
- place (5) — against a supplied GEOMETRY, not always a mesh: on-surface,
  plantable, drop-to-surface, align-to-surface take a mesh (feed them
  `meshPrimitive`); along-curve takes a curve (feed it a path)
- write (8) — set attributes: height-slope, density-from-noise,
  random-scale, random-yaw, color-from-attribute, local-density,
  instances-by-species, orient-along-path

Three rules an agent needs before choosing one:

1. **A `threshold` mask and a probabilistic `density` thin are not the
   same thing.** A threshold gives connected regions with hard edges; a
   probability gives soft-edged clouds of individual points.
2. **Per-instance variation is counter-intuitive.** Two instances of one
   primitive have different node ids, so anything context-seeded
   (scatter, jitter, randomField) differs automatically — but NOISE does
   not unless its own spec asks, and no exposed seed param can make it:
   a noise field's seed lives in its `opts`, which admits a literal or the
   tagged `{ "from": "node", "variant": N }` and nothing else (a
   `{ fn: "param" }` reaches argument positions, and that one `variant`
   slot). Every noise-bearing primitive therefore exposes `variant`, an
   OFFSET added to the noise sample position — the same word one level out
   and a different mechanism from the seed form's slot number — and says
   so in its description. `frequency` is the matching multiplier on that
   position.
3. **An exposed param's default is a plain value, never a `Field`,** and
   every cook writes it inward — so a primitive's characteristic field
   lives on its inner node and the scalars that field reads back are what
   get exposed. Field-capable params are marked in the catalog and accept
   a field spec as their VALUE. There are two routes into a field spec:
   attribute plumbing (a `setAttribute` upstream, `removeAttribute`
   downstream) is the older, and a targetless param the spec reads as
   `{ fn: "param", name }` is the newer and is what every shipped
   primitive now uses. Which one is right is a domain question: a value
   the GRAPH computes is an attribute, one a CALLER supplies is a param.
   A targetless param takes a Field as its value too — it is spliced into
   the expression that reads the name — so "uniform over the cook" is not
   the dividing line.

## Key invariants and contracts

- Determinism: all randomness derives from seeds via PCG32 + 32-bit hash
  combining. Same graph + seed = byte-identical output across runs,
  platforms, cook orders, and streaming paths. Seed chain: graph seed ->
  node seed = hashCombine(graphSeed, hashString(nodeId)) -> per-point
  hashCombine(seed, index, axis). No Math.random anywhere. The chain's
  last link — the one that turns a u32 into a number you can use — is
  `hashFloat(h)`, and it is a public function precisely so a host does
  not invent a second one: it takes the TOP 24 bits (`(h >>> 8) * 2**-24`),
  which puts the result in [0, 1), makes it exactly representable as an
  f32, and keeps it BELOW 1 once stored in a Float32Array, where the
  obvious `h / 2**32` can round up to exactly 1 and put a "probability"
  outside its own range. `randomField` resolves through it, so anything
  reproducing a draw the graph made on the host side agrees with the
  graph by construction rather than by luck.
- The ONE exception to that chain: `pointScatterInWorld`'s lattice is a
  function of its own `seed` param alone — the graph seed is not an input
  at all, exactly as a noise field carries its seed inside its own spec.
  It is deliberate: `graph.setSeed` inside a level's `bind`, a CLI
  `--seed` override or a rename would otherwise silently DE-ANCHOR it, and
  a de-anchored world source fails only at seams. The cost you must plan
  for is the lost node-id decorrelation — two such nodes with identical
  params scatter IDENTICAL points, so give each layer its own value
  (`hashCombine(ctx.worldSeed, 1)` for trees, `...2` for rocks).
- Per-point randomness keys on point IDENTITY, not array index, wherever
  a point must decide the same way under any window: `filterByDensity`
  (probabilistic), `jitterPoints`, `randomField` on the POINT domain, and
  the tiebreaks in `selfPrune` and `pointNeighborhood`. Identity is the
  stored position bits plus the point's `seed` attribute, so an upstream
  filter that renumbers everything cannot move a survivor's draw, and two
  points sharing a position AND a seed are one point to that draw. A
  PRIMITIVE is named the same way, one level up: `randomField` on the
  primitive domain keys on the order-independent fold of its own points'
  identities, so a reordered network re-rolls nothing and an edge agrees
  with its reverse — at the price that two primitives over the same point
  SET collide whatever their vertex order (a quad ABCD and a quad ABDC
  draw alike). The exclusions are principled, not oversights: on the
  vertex and detail domains `randomField` still keys on index, because a
  vertex is a point AND a place within a primitive — a different question
  nothing has asked yet — and detail is one element; and `surfaceSample`
  still keys on index because it manufactures its own candidates rather
  than receiving them.
- Identity keying makes those nodes indifferent to the WINDOW, not to
  their own seed. `filterByDensity`, `jitterPoints` and any field param
  resolving `randomField` or `nodeSeed` still fold in the node seed, so
  wiring a per-cell `ctx.seed` into one of them de-anchors a chain one
  node after the source. Seed them from the cell-invariant `ctx.worldSeed` /
  `ctx.levelSeed`, or leave them at their defaults. See docs/authoring.md,
  "Content that must NOT vary per cell", for the full table.
- Purity: node execute treats inputs as immutable and uses only its
  derived seed. The executor memoizes on exactly (type, params, seed,
  input revs); params hash structurally (Fields by their stable key,
  DataItems by rev — geometry is never deep-hashed).
- Cook results are immutable: `CookResult` collections alias live cache
  internals. Clone with `cloneGeometry(geo)` before mutating. Arrays
  bound into params (e.g. dataInput `items`) are captured by reference —
  treat as frozen after binding; bind a fresh array to change data.
- Topology is fragile and its loss is silent: every filter node that can
  remove points routes through `gatherPoints`, which rebuilds the point
  domain and drops primitive topology with it, and `mergePoints` and
  `partitionByAttribute` do the same. Three filters are exempt —
  `projectToPlane` (clones, removes nothing) and the primitive filters
  `filterPrimitivesByBounds` and `filterPrimitivesByAttribute` (they
  filter the PRIMITIVE domain, so the survivors keep their topology). A path that passes through one of the
  others stops being a path, with no warning at the point of loss — see
  "Paths".
- Column lifetime: an evaluated field Column may alias attribute storage
  and is valid only until the geometry is mutated or resized; results
  memoize per EvalContext object, so make a fresh context after mutation.
- Cache invalidation is automatic via memo keys (param edits, seed
  changes, input rev changes, subgraph inner-graph edits). Cancelling a
  cook (AbortSignal -> CookCancelledError) keeps finished nodes' caches.

## World streaming (hierarchical runtime)

`new World({ seed, levels, maxCellsPerLevel?, onCellReady?, onCellEvicted? })`
streams grid cells per level around a viewpoint. Levels are ordered
coarse to fine (optionally one leading unbounded level); each is a
`LevelDef`:

- `name`, `graph`, `bind(graph, ctx)` — required.
- `cellSize`: number (cell edge, world units) or `"unbounded"` (one
  global cell, must be the first level).
- `cellMode?`: `"xz"` (default — square XZ cells, unbounded in Y,
  coords `[cx, cz]`), `"xyz"` (cube cells, coords `[cx, cy, cz]`,
  radii in full XYZ distance), or `"path"` (ARC LENGTH along a
  centreline: a cell is the half-open range `[sMin, sMax)`, coord
  `[cs]`, the table cut into `round(length / cellSize)` equal sectors so
  the seam falls exactly at `s = 0`). Nesting: like under like (a
  `"path"` child maps to the parent SECTOR containing its arc midpoint,
  and nested `"path"` levels must declare the same `path` table);
  `"xyz"` under `"xz"` uses the containing XZ column as parent; `"xz"`
  under a bounded `"xyz"` parent is rejected at construction, and so is
  `"path"` mixed with either world-space mode in either direction — an
  arc sector is a tube along a curve, so no square cell contains it and
  it contains none, which also means a bounded square level and a
  `"path"` level cannot coexist in one World. An unbounded parent
  accepts any mode. Coarse-to-fine `cellSize` is checked WITHIN a mode
  family (arc lengths against arc lengths).
- `path?`: `{ length, closed }` — required for `"path"`, refused
  otherwise. A RULER, not a curve: the World never sees the centreline,
  and there is no second copy of it to disagree with the graph's. It is
  STATIC and cannot come from a parent's outputs — the wanted set is
  built before any cell cooks, so a parent-sourced table would make
  wanted-set membership a function of cook state.
- `generationRadius?`: cells cook when their center enters this radius.
  Required (positive) for bounded levels; omit for an unbounded level
  (a value is accepted and ignored there). On a `"path"` level it is an
  ARC distance from the anchor to the sector's nearest bound, and IS the
  symmetric window: exactly `aheadArc = behindArc = generationRadius`.
- `retainRadius?`: eviction hysteresis, default generationRadius * 1.25.
  Refused on a `"path"` level that states a directional window.
- `aheadArc?` / `behindArc?` (`"path"` only): the directional window, in
  arc units forward and back of the anchor. Both must be stated, both
  finite and >= 0 (0 is legal — it still wants the sector the anchor is
  standing in, and nothing further on that side), and they REPLACE
  `generationRadius`, which is refused alongside them. "Ahead" is
  increasing arc, so a level travelled the other way mirrors its window
  rather than passing a reverse flag. Cook order ranks by gap / that
  half's depth, not by raw arc, so a starved budget is not spent on road
  already driven. A window longer than a closed table clamps to it
  (every sector wanted once); on an open table it runs off the ends.
- `retainAheadArc?` / `retainBehindArc?`: per-half hysteresis, each
  defaulting to its own half * 1.25 and required to be >= its own half.
  One scalar across two unequal halves either inflates the short half or
  strips the long half's band, which is why `retainRadius` is refused
  with a directional window rather than applied to both.
- `cookOutputs?`: cook only these declared outputs of the graph per
  cell (per-output cooking; names validated at construction). Omit to
  cook all.

Before each cell cook, `bind(graph, ctx)` wires the `CellContext` into
the graph — the only channel for cell data. `ctx` is a discriminated
union on `cellMode`: `{ cellMode, coord, min, max, levelIndex,
levelName, worldSeed, levelSeed, seed, parent? }` with 2D coord/min/max
for `"xz"` (and unbounded) levels, 3D for `"xyz"`. A `"path"` cell
carries `{ coord: [cs], sMin, sMax, pathLength, closed }` and NO
`min`/`max`, deliberately: an arc sector is a curved tube with no
world-space box, and a third `min` under the same name would let the
usual `cellMode === "xyz" ? … : (xz)` else-branch read a 1-tuple's
`min[1]` as a z that was never there. Omitting it breaks that at COMPILE
time; `xzCell(ctx)` (exported) is the narrowing for the square case, and
a `"path"` bind narrows on `ctx.cellMode` and reads `sMin`/`sMax`.
Three seeds, and picking the wrong one is the classic streaming bug:

- `seed` — PER CELL, = hashCombine(worldSeed, levelIndex, ...coord)
  (every cell coordinate is hashed — `[cs]` alone on a `"path"` level;
  the chain's length prefix keeps the 1-, 2- and 3-tuple arities from
  colliding). Wire it into every stochastic node whose content is MEANT
  to differ per cell.
- `worldSeed` — the `World`'s own `seed`, identical in every cell of
  every level. The coarsest cell-INVARIANT anchor.
- `levelSeed` — = hashCombine(worldSeed, levelIndex), identical within a
  level. Use it where `worldSeed` would work but two levels running the
  same graph should get unrelated worlds rather than the same one. On an
  unbounded level `levelSeed` and `seed` are the same number.

Contract: derive params only from ctx. Sanctioned seeding: set seed
params per node (vary with hashCombine(ctx.seed, n); setAttribute's
`seed` param folds in as hashCombine(nodeSeed, seed), 0 = unchanged), or
reseed the whole graph via `graph.setSeed(...)` inside bind — memo keys
include seeds and bind-time writes never count as user edits, so neither
causes phantom recooks. Parent-cell outputs arrive as
`ctx.parent.outputs`; inject them via a dataInput node. `await
world.update([x, y, z], { budgetMs?, signal?, maxCooksPerUpdate?,
anchors? })` cooks nearest-first, evicts by retainRadius + LRU, and
reports { cooked, evicted, pending }. `world.invalidate(level?, coord?)`
forces recooks; parent recooks cascade staleness to children
automatically.

`anchors` is `{ [levelName]: s }`, the arc position of each `"path"`
level, and every `"path"` level REQUIRES a finite entry: such a level
ignores the viewpoint entirely, so the anchor is the only way it gets a
position. A missing entry, a non-finite value, an unknown level name, or
a name that is not a `"path"` level throws `WorldValidationError`, all
checked before any cell of the update cooks. On a closed table the
anchor wraps (any real number is in range and the `s = 0` seam is not a
boundary, matching `pathRuns`/`arcTile`); on an open one it is used as
given and the seam IS a boundary. A mixed World streams in one call: the
world point drives the `"xz"`/`"xyz"` levels, each anchor its own path
level. An anchor is a COORDINATE (like the viewpoint); the window is
POLICY and stays on `LevelDef` — a per-frame window would make the
wanted set a function of the frame that asked. Nothing projects a world
point onto the centreline: the caller already knows its station, and a
projection would need a stated tie-break at every crossover.

### Cross-cell content: halos and ownership

A cell never fetches from a sibling — `World` exposes no sibling
accessor and neighbours are LRU-evictable, so anything that must look
past a cell edge DERIVES it from world coordinates instead. The pattern,
in three moves:

1. **Source it anchored.** `pointScatterInWorld`, seeded from
   `ctx.worldSeed` / `ctx.levelSeed` (never `ctx.seed`, which would make
   every cell an unrelated world and the guarantee empty).
2. **Ask for the halo.** Widen the query: `boundsMin = ctx.min - halo`,
   `boundsMax = ctx.max + halo`. The extra ring is byte-identical to what
   the neighbour owns whether or not it has ever cooked. Run the
   measurement that needs it (`pointNeighborhood`, `sampleNearestPoint`,
   `transferAttribute`) over the WIDE cloud.
3. **Clip to ownership.** `filterByBounds` at the default `halfOpen`
   boundary, bound to the UNWIDENED `ctx.min`/`ctx.max`, so two abutting
   cells claim a shared-face point exactly once between them.

The finite-halo restriction is real, and stricter than "local". The
sharp question is not "does this op look local" but **how many HOPS of
dependency it takes before an answer is settled**, and there is a
three-rung ladder:

- **Zero hops — halo-exact, and the easiest case.** The answer reads only
  stored values of the elements it names, and consults no third element.
  `connectPoints` is the type specimen: whether A and B are an edge is a
  distance between two stored positions, so a cell holding every point
  within `radius` of its own rectangle decides its edges EXACTLY at
  `haloWidth >= radius`. (`relativeNeighborhood` looks like it adds a hop
  and does not: its witness must lie inside the pair's own neighbourhood,
  so it is already in the halo.)
- **One hop — halo-exact at a stated width.** The answer reads its
  neighbours' STORED values, but not its neighbours' answers.
  `pointNeighborhood` is bounded by `radius`; `selfPrune`'s
  `localMaximum` rule decides each point from its immediate neighbours
  alone, which is why that mode is the halo-exact one.
- **Unbounded — no halo works, at any width.** The answer depends on
  another element's ANSWER, and the chain has no bound. A greedy prune is
  the case: a point survives because its neighbour did not, because ITS
  neighbour did. So is a minimum spanning tree (an edge is in the tree
  iff no lighter PATH connects its ends — which is why `connectPoints`
  offers `relativeNeighborhood`, a local lune test that CONTAINS an MST,
  rather than an MST mode) and so is a shortest path. A global rank or a
  population total is worse still: no reach bound exists to widen to.

Check the node's own entry in docs/nodes.md for which rule is halo-exact
and what width it needs. One wrinkle on step 3 above: when the op emitted
TOPOLOGY, ownership is a PRIMITIVE-domain decision — `filterPrimitivesByBounds`
on the unwidened rectangle at `vertex: "first"`, same `halfOpen` boundary —
because `filterByBounds` there would drop the topology rather than trim it
(see "Networks").
Worked example with code: docs/authoring.md,
"Content that must NOT vary per cell".
Runnable: `demos/infinite-world` (its "halo" and "world-anchored"
toggles reproduce each failure live) and
`graphs/basics-scatter-in-world.json`.

## GPU field evaluation (pcg-ts/gpu)

The serializable field-expression grammar (previous section) is the GPU
surface: every fn compiles to WGSL.

DESCRIBING vs RUNNING — two questions since v0.9, do not conflate them:
- `getFieldSpec(field)` answers "can this field be described": a spec
  for both `fieldFromJson` fields (AUTHORED) and combinator fields
  (DERIVED), `undefined` only for a `makeField` closure, anything
  composed over one, or a tree past 256 levels.
- Device eligibility is NARROWER: an authored spec always, a derived
  spec only when the resolver advertises `acceptDerivedSpecs: true`
  (default false). With it off a derived-spec field evaluates on the
  CPU and counts a `"derived-spec"` fallback — NOT `"no-spec"`, which
  now means genuinely undescribable.
- Opt-in on purpose: derived and authored forms of one expression
  compile to the same kernel key and the same WGSL and produce the same
  bytes (measured, one adapter), but the GPU path is still a documented
  approximation of the CPU reference. Turning the gate on by default
  would move output bytes for graphs that already pass a resolver and
  never asked, including discrete flips at knife-edge compares. The
  memo salt protects cache correctness, not output stability, so
  adoption is the caller's explicit choice per evaluator.

One eligible field = one compute dispatch over the whole domain
(chunked into several `dispatchWorkgroups` calls past 65535 × 64 ≈
4.19M elements, byte-invisibly). Chains of fusable nodes go further:
they cook as one device-resident run with a single readback (see
"Device-resident runs" below).

Setup (browser):

```ts
import { cook } from "pcg-ts";
import { GpuFieldEvaluator } from "pcg-ts/gpu";
const adapter = await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter();
const device = await adapter.requestDevice();
const gpu = new GpuFieldEvaluator(device, { adapterInfo: adapter.info });
const result = await cook(graph, { gpu });   // CookOptions.gpu
```

Node: `npm i -D webgpu` (Dawn bindings; the library has no dependency
on it), then `const adapter = await create([]).requestAdapter()` with
`import { create } from "webgpu"`.

Surface:

- `GpuFieldResolver` (core interface, no WebGPU types): `{ cacheSalt:
  string; residentTerminals?: readonly string[]; acceptDerivedSpecs?:
  boolean; resolveField(field, ctx, stats?): Promise<Column> | null;
  planRun?; executeRun? }` — `acceptDerivedSpecs` is the SINGLE source
  of truth for derived-spec eligibility: the executor reads it to
  decide both the memo-key salt and fusion, and the resolver must act
  on exactly the same value, or it produces GPU bytes under a CPU memo
  key. The two run methods are optional and
  detailed under "Device-resident runs" below; absence degrades to
  per-node cooking with identical bytes.
  `null` is returned synchronously for ineligible fields — the caller
  falls back to the CPU `evaluateField` and the reason is counted. A
  non-null return commits to GPU: it resolves to a freshly allocated
  column (never a view of attribute storage) with the same element type
  and tuple size the CPU would produce; a rejection is an error (device
  failure), never a silent fallback.
- `CookOptions.gpu?: GpuFieldResolver` / `WorldOptions.gpu?` /
  `UpdateOptions.gpu?` (update wins, threaded to every cell cook) /
  `captureAsync(geo, domain, field, seed?, gpu?, stats?)` — the
  graph-free entry point; without `gpu` it is byte-identical to
  `capture`.
- `CookStats.gpu` (present exactly when the cook was given a resolver;
  includes nested subgraph-cook work): `{ dispatches,
  pipelinesCompiled, pipelineCacheHits, residentRuns, fusedNodes,
  readbacksSaved, fallbacks: Record<reason, count> }`.
  `dispatches` = **kernels**, one per resolved field column plus one
  apply kernel per fused member — NOT `dispatchWorkgroups` calls; a
  chunked kernel still counts once (a 4.3M-point 4-member run reports
  4 while issuing 8). Exactly one kernel counts more than once: a
  MULTI-ASSET spawner terminal dispatches once per asset present in the
  input, over that asset's element range and into that asset's output
  buffer, so the unit is (step, asset), not step. Those are distinct
  dispatches over disjoint ranges, not chunks of one range. A
  constant-`assetId` spawn has exactly one asset and still counts 1, so
  v0.7 numbers stay comparable. The complete fallback-reason
  vocabulary:
  - `no-spec` — the field cannot be described at all: a `makeField`
    closure, anything composed over one, a tree past 256 levels, or an
    argument the grammar's parser rejects
  - `derived-spec` — the field describes itself, but its spec was
    DERIVED by the combinator API and this resolver does not advertise
    `acceptDerivedSpecs`. Scoped to the PER-FIELD seam only: a node the
    same setting keeps out of a fused run is not counted again at the
    fusion gate, since its fields still fall back per-field and one
    cause reported twice would read as two
  - `compile-error` — spec cannot lower to WGSL against the geometry's
    attribute layout (missing attribute, a string attribute reached by
    `attribute` rather than by `attributeIs`/`byAttribute`, tuple size > 4, non-finite
    f32 constant)
  - `too-many-buffers` — kernel needs > 8 storage buffers (more than 7
    attribute inputs + the output; baseline WebGPU limit)
  - `run-plan-failed` — some member of a resident run cannot be
    compiled into the pipeline (unknown resident kind, field compile
    error, tuple/layout mismatch, missing standard attribute, buffer
    limit, a spawn over the instance budget or naming a bad
    `assetAttr`/`colorAttr`, a spawn naming `instanceAttrs` channels without the
    evaluator's `deviceInstanceAttrs`
    (the one entry here that is not a mistake — a capability gate, see
    the device-resident instancing section),
    or an `attributeIs`/`byAttribute` anywhere in the run —
    its kernel compiles and dispatches fine on the per-node path, but
    the uniform it reads is a string-table index of the geometry being
    cooked and a PLAN has only attribute descriptors and a count).
    Counted once per rejected run; every
    member then cooks per-node, including surfacing the identical CPU
    error for genuinely invalid params. That is deliberate reuse: an
    over-budget or mis-named spawn adds NO new fallback reason, and
    since the device path never words the message itself the two paths
    cannot word it differently.
  - `run-too-large` — a run's resident working set exceeds
    `maxResidentBytes`. Counted once per rejected run.
  - NODE-level opt-outs (`ResidentDesc.eligible` returning a reason
    string) are part of this vocabulary in principle, but the standard
    node library declares NONE. Every reason a standard node stays off
    the device today is one of the per-field or per-run reasons above.
    v0.7's `spawn-asset-attr` was the only one and v0.8 retired it:
    `spawnInstances` is device-resident with `assetAttr` set as well.
    `instanceAttrs` is deliberately NOT a node-level gate either: an
    `eligible` predicate would keep `spawnInstances` off EVERY resident
    run in the graph, where the run planner rejects only the run that
    actually names channels.
  - Element count is NEVER a fallback reason; `dispatch-too-large` no
    longer exists (chunking removed it).
- `NodeDef.gpu?: "fields" | "always"` — GPU-adoption marker. `"fields"`
  on `setAttribute`, `transformPoints`, `jitterPoints`,
  `orientAlongVector`, `surfaceSample`, `volumeSample`; `"always"` on
  subgraph defs (they forward the resolver to inner cooks and their
  counters land in the outermost sink). When a cook has a resolver and
  such a node has a live Field param this resolver WOULD accept
  (authored, or derived with the gate on), the memo key gains
  `|gpu:<cacheSalt>` — so toggling gpu never serves bytes produced by
  the other path, while nodes with no acceptable field param keep their
  cache hits across the toggle. The marker is conservative: it applies
  for eligible-but-uncompilable fields too (over-invalidation; bytes
  stay CPU-identical). `GpuFieldEvaluator`'s salt is
  `"gpu2|<vendor>|<architecture>|<device>|<description>"` (format
  version + adapter identity; missing fields become `?`) — bytes from
  different devices never serve each other. The executor appends
  `+derived` to that salt when `acceptDerivedSpecs` is on and appends
  NOTHING when it is off, so two evaluators on one adapter that
  disagree about the gate cannot collide in the memo cache, and every
  pre-v0.9 key is byte-identical.
- `GpuFieldEvaluatorOptions`: `adapterInfo?` (salt identity when the
  device exposes none); `maxResidentBytes?` (default 512 MiB — the
  resident-run working-set bound); `maxPooledBytes?` (default 256 MiB —
  idle bytes the buffer pool retains; `0` disables retention);
  `maxElementsPerDispatch?` (chunk size override, byte-invisible,
  intended for tests forcing chunk seams — production code leaves it
  unset; default `65535 × workgroupSize` = 4 194 240 at wg 64);
  `deviceInstances?` (default false — opt in to device-resident
  instance transforms and their colours; see "Device-resident
  instancing" below);
  `acceptDerivedSpecs?` (default false — opt in to resolving fields
  whose spec was DERIVED by the combinator API; see "DESCRIBING vs
  RUNNING" above). Both are advertised on the resolver
  (`evaluator.residentTerminals`, `evaluator.acceptDerivedSpecs`) so
  the executor and the resolver decide from one value.
- `evaluator.dispose()` destroys pooled (idle) buffers only; in-flight
  buffers stay valid and re-pool on release and the evaluator remains
  usable (pipeline/kernel caches untouched). DETACHED buffers (device
  transform handles) are untouched too — the pool does not own them.
  `evaluator.poolStats` → `{ buffersCreated, buffersReused,
  buffersDestroyed, pooledBuffers, pooledBytes, buffersDetached,
  detachedBuffers, detachedBytes }`.
- Pipelines cache on the evaluator instance (keyed by kernel
  specialization key = codegen version + spec key + attribute layout)
  and persist across cooks; `pipelineCacheSize` getter for tools.
- `compileFieldSpec(spec, { attributes })` and `supportedGpuFieldFns()`
  are exported for direct WGSL inspection; compile errors are
  actionable (they name the spec node and list what is supported).
- World note: toggling gpu between updates does NOT recook stored
  cells (cell staleness is version-based); provenance protects the
  graph memo layer whenever a cell actually recooks.

Device-resident runs (fusion):

- Opt-in through two OPTIONAL resolver methods, both or neither — the
  executor fuses only when it finds both, so a v0.5-style resolver
  gets exactly the per-node behavior and identical bytes:
  - `planRun?(members: readonly ResidentMemberDesc[], ctx:
    ResidentRunContext, stats?): object | null` — synchronous and
    device-free. `null` = cannot fuse; the resolver counts the reason
    and every member cooks per-node. The returned plan is opaque to the
    executor.
  - `executeRun?(plan: object, input: ResidentRunInput, stats?):
    Promise<ResidentRunResult>` — commits to device execution; a
    rejection is an error, never a silent fallback (except the standard
    cancellation error when `input.signal` aborted). Its `geo` must be
    structurally indistinguishable from cooking the members
    sequentially: same attribute set, shapes, defaults, insertion
    order, string tables, topology; untouched attributes pass through
    byte-identically.
  - `ResidentMemberDesc` = `{ id, type, kind, params, seed }` (`kind`
    from the node def's `resident` descriptor, `seed` exactly what the
    CPU execute would receive). `ResidentRunContext` = `{ attributes:
    Record<name, { type, tupleSize }>, count }`.
- Fusable CHAIN kinds (exactly four, all count-preserving, one geometry
  in / one geometry out): `setAttribute` (numeric mode only — not
  `type: "string"`, `domain: "point"`, empty `values`, empty
  `stringValue`), `transformPoints`, `jitterPoints`,
  `orientAlongVector`. Plus one TERMINAL kind, `spawnInstances`
  (`ResidentDesc.terminal: true`): it may be a run's LAST member, a
  chain never continues through it, and it joins a run only when the
  resolver lists its kind in `residentTerminals` — see
  "Device-resident instancing" below. Additionally, for EVERY member:
  every `Field` in its param tree must carry a spec this resolver
  accepts (authored always; derived only under `acceptDerivedSpecs`),
  so the gate widens which chains fuse as well as which fields resolve.
- Boundary rules — the executor takes MAXIMAL linear chains and stops
  when: the tail has ≠ 1 outgoing connection (any fan-out, counting
  connections to nodes outside this cook's selection), the tail carries
  a declared graph output, the consumer is outside the cooked
  selection, the consumer is not fusable, or the consumer's incoming
  set is not exactly the tail. A chain of length 1 is not a run —
  EXCEPT a lone TERMINAL, which is (see "Device-resident instancing").
  Detection is conservative: it under-fuses, never over-fuses. An
  interior node with external consumers becomes a run terminal with its
  own readback — fusion never changes which bytes the graph observes.
- Cache contract: ONLY the run terminal caches, under
  `run1|gpu:<cacheSalt>|i<first member inputSig>|m[type|s<seed>|p<paramHash>|x<memoKey>]…`
  (one `m[...]` tuple per member, in order). Interior members hold NO
  entry while fused (any stale per-node entry is cleared). Editing any
  member recooks exactly that run; siblings and upstream stay cached.
  Run keys and per-node keys (`<type>|s…`) can never collide, so
  neither path serves the other's bytes — but a node holds ONE memo
  slot, so flipping gpu on/off (or fusion on/off) recooks the chain
  every time BY DESIGN. Benchmark from cold caches.
- Memory: working set = Σ resident slot bytes over every epoch + Σ
  field-temporary column bytes (held for the WHOLE run, not just their
  member) + readback staging bytes, checked against `maxResidentBytes`
  at plan time. Logical bytes only: pow2 pool bucketing can allocate up
  to 2×, and the 12-byte per-chunk uniforms are not counted.
- Cost model: a CONSTANT param (plain number or number tuple) costs a
  16-byte uniform slot and NO dispatch — only field-valued params
  materialize an `n`-element column. Measured at v0.6.1 on the
  five-node fusable chain that was then a demo page of its own and is
  now the corpus graph `examples-gpu-fields.json`: 120 bytes per point
  (was 212) and 9 member kernels (was 12). Constant values live in the
  uniform, never in generated WGSL: the apply-kernel key encodes only
  which params are constant, their tuple sizes, and their slots, so
  editing a constant hits the pipeline cache instead of recompiling.
  A kernel carries at most `MAX_APPLY_CONST_SLOTS` (4) constant slots.
- Third-party `resident` kinds: `NodeDef.resident?: { kind: string;
  eligible?(params): boolean | string; terminal?: boolean }`.
  `eligible` runs outside the executor's error wrapping — it must be
  cheap, pure, and total; an exception there escapes `cook()`
  unwrapped. Returning a non-empty STRING means the same as `false`
  (does not fuse) but names the reason, which the executor counts once
  per cook in `fallbacks` under exactly that key — use it for
  author-actionable cases, plain `false` otherwise. `terminal: true`
  permits output pins beyond the single geometry one (the resolver must
  then model every extra pin) and requires the resolver to advertise
  the kind in `residentTerminals`.

Device-resident instancing (pcg-ts/gpu + pcg-ts/three) — v0.7.0,
multi-asset since v0.8.0:

- Opt in: `new GpuFieldEvaluator(device, { deviceInstances: true })`.
  That sets `evaluator.residentTerminals = ["spawnInstances"]`; default
  `[]`, and with `[]` the spawner cooks byte-for-byte as it always has.
- Terminal contract. ANY `spawnInstances` may end a run — constant
  `assetId` and non-empty `assetAttr` alike (v0.7 restricted this to
  `assetAttr === ""`; v0.8 does not). The node declares NO `eligible`
  gate. The run appends a compose-TRS kernel writing one column-major
  4x4 f32 per point (`count * 64` bytes, exactly the `InstanceBatch`
  layout) into ONE BUFFER PER ASSET, each of which it then
  `BufferPool.detach`es. With `colorAttr` set, the SAME kernel also
  gathers RGB into a second buffer per asset — no second traversal
  exists, so the two cannot fall out of step. A LONE spawner IS a run under the opt-in (the
  single-node exception: fusion is the only way to produce device
  output at all). When `ResidentRunContext.needsGeometry` is false —
  the terminal's geometry pin is neither connected nor a declared
  output — the run does NO readback: no `mapAsync`, no staging buffer,
  no CPU copy of P/rot/scale. `stats.readbacksSaved` then contributes
  `members`, the one case where
  `readbacksSaved === fusedNodes - residentRuns` fails.
- What the caller receives: the terminal's instances pin carries an
  `InstancesItem` with `deviceBatches?: readonly DeviceInstanceBatch[]`
  (`{ residency: "device", assetId, count, transforms, colors? }`), ONE
  ENTRY PER ASSET in the batch order specified below, NOT
  `batches`. Reading `.batches` on it THROWS (naming both fixes) —
  probe with `isDeviceResidentInstances(item)` or
  `item.deviceBatches !== undefined` FIRST. `transforms` is a
  `DeviceTransformsHandle`: `{ backend: string; byteLength: number;
  disposed: boolean; resource: unknown; dispose(): void }` — opaque,
  never a `Float32Array`. `deviceTransformsBuffer(handle)`
  (`pcg-ts/gpu`) narrows `resource` to the backend buffer; bind exactly
  `byteLength` bytes from offset 0 (pool buckets to pow2 — the tail is
  uninitialized). Wrong backend or a disposed handle throws.
- `colors` is present only when `colorAttr` is set, is the same handle
  type, and DOES NOT HAVE THE CPU LAYOUT. WGSL `array<vec3<f32>>` pads
  to a 16-byte stride, so the device buffer is 4 f32 per instance
  (`count * 16` bytes) where the CPU `InstanceBatch.colors` packs 3
  (`count * 12`); instance k is at
  `4k..4k+2` and the kernel writes `4k+3` as a literal `0f` rather than
  leaving it undefined. Anyone extending the device path must respect
  that stride — it is the one place the two layouts legitimately
  differ.
- NAMED CHANNELS ARE NOT COMPOSED BY THIS KERNEL, and their device
  production is OPT-IN. Read that as a statement about who binds the
  buffers and nothing else — it is NOT a statement that a channel cannot
  reach a GPU, and it is NOT a statement that the cook runs on your
  frame. See the two scoping notes at the end of this bullet before
  planning around it. `instanceAttrs` is the ONE `spawnInstances` param
  whose device production is opt-in, and it is the one spawner condition
  in this section that is NOT about a mistake.
  DEFAULT OFF, which is what it always was: a spawn naming any channel
  REJECTS the whole resident run as `run-plan-failed`; the CPU spawner
  then serves the ENTIRE terminal — the transforms it composes there, its
  colour AND its channels — so nothing is dropped and nothing is silent,
  and the rejection is counted in `CookStats.gpu.fallbacks` like every
  other. The counter key is ALL a caller observes: the planner words a
  sentence but `PlanRejection` carries only the reason, so that wording
  never leaves `planResidentRun` — assert on the counter, not on a
  message.
  WITH `deviceInstanceAttrs: true` on the `GpuFieldEvaluator` (which
  requires `deviceInstances` and throws if passed alone), each channel is
  gathered into its own retained device buffer beside the transforms, by
  its OWN kernel rather than more bindings on the compose one — whose
  widest form already binds seven storage buffers (P, rot, scale,
  transforms, the permutation, the colour source, the colour output)
  against the baseline `maxStorageBuffersPerShaderStage` of 8, so folding
  channels in would have bought exactly one. The gather binds both sides
  as `array<u32>` and moves raw words, so every COMPONENT matches the CPU
  column bit for bit; an itemSize-3 channel additionally carries a pad
  slot the CPU column has no room for, per WGSL's 16-byte vec3 stride.
  WHY IT IS A SEPARATE FLAG, and this is the whole of it: it moves an
  OBLIGATION. `pcg-ts/three`'s device adapter binds the instance matrix
  and the reserved colour and refuses every other channel by name, so a
  graph that names channels and renders through that adapter works today
  only because the planner rejects. Turn the flag on and you bind the
  buffers yourself from `batch.attributes[name].handle.resource`. The
  node declares no `eligible` gate either way — a gate would keep
  `spawnInstances` off every resident run in the graph, where the planner
  rejects only the run that actually names channels.
  Consequence for parity: with the flag off such a spawn has NO parity
  class at all, there being no device output to compare, transforms
  included; with it on, the channels are a bit-exact gather rather than a
  tolerance class, while the transforms keep their documented one.
  SCOPING NOTE 1 — RENDERING IS SUPPORTED. The CPU batch this fallback
  produces carries every channel, and `toInstancedMeshes` binds each as
  an `InstancedBufferAttribute` of its own name; it is renderer-agnostic,
  so a `WebGPURenderer` draws it exactly as a `WebGLRenderer` does. A
  CPU-produced column reaching a WebGPU/TSL material is the SUPPORTED
  path for per-instance data in a shader and nothing in this section
  touches it. The library ships the data, not the shader — no `three/tsl`
  import, `normalized`/`gpuType` at three's defaults — so the material is
  the host's to write. DO NOT SET `gpuType` ON AN INTEGER CHANNEL — this
  file said the opposite twice and it was wrong both times. MEASURED on a
  real draw call with a pixel readback: a `Uint32Array` channel arrives
  EXACT with the flag left at three's default. `WebGLAttributes` maps
  `Uint32Array` to `gl.UNSIGNED_INT`, and `WebGLBindingStates` picks the
  integer pointer call as `type === gl.INT || type === gl.UNSIGNED_INT ||
  gpuType === IntType`, so for an integer typed array the flag is
  short-circuited before it is read; the same ids read back
  BYTE-IDENTICALLY unset and with `IntType`. The flag IS load-bearing for
  any integer array NARROWER than 32 bits — `Uint8Array`, how a `bool`
  channel is stored, among them: `gl.UNSIGNED_BYTE` fails both GL-type
  tests, so `IntType` is what selects the integer path, and without it
  the pointer call still succeeds and the DRAW fails
  (`INVALID_OPERATION`). Declare such a channel `in uint`, not `in int`:
  the WebGL2 matching rule is three-way. And the flag is HARMFUL on a
  `Float32Array`, where it makes three call `vertexAttribIPointer` with
  `gl.FLOAT` — not an accepted type there, so `INVALID_ENUM` at the
  pointer call, which then does nothing. THREE'S OWN JSDOC DENIES THIS
  (`BufferAttribute` calls `gpuType` "not configurable for float
  arrays"); the code has no such guard, and the code is what runs.
  `gpuType` is a WebGL concept: native WebGPU takes the vertex format
  from the array's constructor and never reads it (zero occurrences under
  three's `renderers/webgpu/`, which widens a `Uint8Array` to
  `Uint32Array` before upload, so even a bool channel needs no flag
  there). Only the WebGL2 fallback backend consults it, in two places,
  both of which exempt the 32-bit integer arrays anyway. NOT MEASURED HERE: the `Uint8Array` and `Float32Array`
  cases are read out of three's source (r185) and the WebGL2 rules,
  not bound by anything in this repo. What DOES have to agree is the
  shader-side type: declaring a u32 channel as `in float` does not round
  quietly, WebGL2 rejects it LOUDLY. The test pins the loudness — a GL
  error, or nothing drawn — rather than either specific, because the code
  is the driver's; on the adapter this ran on it was `INVALID_OPERATION`
  (0x502) with no fragment written. The 2^24 collision is real but
  belongs to an F32 COLUMN, not to a missing flag: the same four ids
  carried through an f32 column read back `[0, 0, 80, 160]`, two of them
  collapsed onto one. That is the argument for preserving dtype, and it
  is what `demos/lanterns` draws both ways. SCOPE OF "SUPPORTED":
  `demos/lanterns` binds a custom channel and draws with it, and
  `tests/instanceChannelRender.test.ts` issues real draw calls in a
  browser and reads the pixels back under both renderers — measured, no
  longer merely intended. The lone WebGPU-side refusal is the
  DEVICE-RESIDENT adapter (`createWebGpuInstanceAdapter`), which binds
  only the instance matrix and the reserved colour, and which throws on a
  hand-built device batch carrying anything else, naming both ways out
  (drop `deviceInstances` for CPU batches, or bind
  `batch.attributes[name].handle.resource` yourself).
  SCOPING NOTE 2 — THE FALLBACK NEED NOT BE ON THE MAIN THREAD. It is a
  CPU cook, not a main-thread one: `pcg-ts/worker` cooks off-thread and
  ships every channel with the transforms on the transfer list (buffer
  ownership, not a copy), so losing the device path does not by itself
  cost a frame hitch.
- SHARED DEVICE IS MANDATORY. One `GPUDevice` must back both the
  `GpuFieldEvaluator` and the `THREE.WebGPURenderer`: a `GPUBuffer`
  belongs to the device that created it, two devices cannot share one,
  and a WebGL context cannot read a WebGPU buffer at all. Construct as
  `device = await gpuAdapter.requestDevice()` →
  `renderer = new WebGPURenderer({ device })` → `await renderer.init()`
  → `new GpuFieldEvaluator(device, { deviceInstances: true })` →
  `await createWebGpuInstanceAdapter({ renderer, assets })`. A batch
  whose handle's backend is not `"webgpu"` is refused by `build()`.
- Renderer wiring (`pcg-ts/three`): `createWebGpuInstanceAdapter({
  renderer, assets }): Promise<WebGpuInstanceAdapter>` (async — it
  imports `three/webgpu` lazily, so a WebGL app pays nothing), then
  `new WorldThreeBinding({ group, assets, deviceInstances: { adapter,
  bounds? } })`. `bounds(levelName, coord, assetId) => { center, radius
  } | undefined` supplies the sphere out of band, because
  `InstancedMesh.computeBoundingSphere()` would read the (empty) CPU
  matrix array and cull the cell away; `undefined` (or an infinite
  centre, i.e. an unbounded level) disables frustum culling for that
  batch's object instead of guessing, and a non-finite/negative radius
  throws. Called ONCE PER BATCH, not once per cell (v0.8): with one
  sphere per cell every asset inherits the padding of the tallest one,
  so `assetId` is the lever for padding by that asset's own radius.
  Ignoring the third argument keeps the per-cell behaviour and existing
  two-parameter callbacks still type-check.
  Without a `deviceInstances` binding, a device-resident item is an
  ERROR naming both fixes — never a silently empty cell.
  `adapter.stats` → `{ built, released, adopted, liveInstances }`.
- Ownership chain, exactly: pool-owned → `detach` (the run's LAST line,
  after the final cancellation check, so every earlier failure path
  reclaims it) → holder-owned handle → `dispose()`. ONE detach and ONE
  handle PER ASSET, so a multi-asset cell hands out N handles; a
  transfer that fails partway disposes each buffer exactly once.
  Nothing else ever frees them: not the pool, not the memo cache, not
  `GpuFieldEvaluator.dispose()`, not `BufferPool.dispose()`.
  - The GRAPH delivers but never owns: a terminal producing device
    batches writes a `volatile` cache entry (delivered once, then
    refused by the hit path), so device-resident output is NEVER
    memoized and every cook mints a fresh handle. Memoizing would pin
    device memory for the graph's lifetime and hand one handle to two
    owners. A handle no delivered collection carries — or one from a
    failed/cancelled cook — is disposed by the cook, not stranded.
  - `WorldThreeBinding` is the owner of last resort: it refcounts
    handles BY IDENTITY and disposes at the last release only. Identity
    is load-bearing — a child cell forwarding its parent's outputs
    holds the SAME handle object, so parent/child eviction is safe in
    either order. Four release paths: evict, recook (new handles
    retained before old released, so a shared handle survives the
    swap), partial build failure (handles retained for the WHOLE cell
    up front, released in the catch), and `binding.dispose()`.
  - The ADAPTER never disposes a handle; it owns only the
    `InstancedMesh` and its attribute. `adapter.release(object)` frees
    those without destroying the adopted buffer.
  - `dispose()` twice is a no-op, never a double free. Reading
    `resource` after dispose throws.
  - Leaks are VISIBLE: an un-disposed handle stays counted in
    `evaluator.poolStats.detachedBuffers` / `.detachedBytes`; the
    binding reports the same population as `binding.deviceHandleCount`
    / `.deviceHandleBytes` — since v0.8 one handle per BATCH (per asset
    in a cell), not one per cell; both count DISTINCT handles, so a
    handle shared across cells counts once. Steady state over a
    fly-through, not climb.
    Cross-check the COUNTS only: pool bytes are pow2 bucket sizes,
    binding bytes are the logical `count * 64` payload, so the two byte
    totals differ permanently and by design.
  - `deviceHandleBytes` is a LEAK METER, NOT VRAM. It is a lower bound
    on device occupancy and since v0.8 a loose one: the pool buckets to
    the next power of two with a 256-BYTE FLOOR (start at 256, double
    until >= the requested size; internal, no exported symbol), and a
    multi-asset spawn takes one buffer per asset, so a cell with four
    small batches pays four roundings instead of one — a 3-instance
    batch is 192 logical bytes in a 256-byte bucket, a 20-instance
